The curtains have officially opened on Design Week Lagos, a citywide celebration of architecture, interior design, product design, and furniture design. The event, which is in its fifth edition, brings together designers, artists, and creatives from across the continent to showcase their work and share their ideas.
This year’s theme, “Made in Africa, Shaping Industries, Shaping Futures,” highlights the importance of design in shaping industries and futures.
Founder of Design Week Lagos, Titi Ogufere, spoke about the inspiration behind this year’s theme. “We feel like it’s essential for people to understand, especially in Nigeria, the power of design and what design does in developing any society,” she said. “If you look at what’s happening, we’re actually ripe in Africa. Most people can’t afford normal furniture, so we have to look inwards, begin to develop what we have, from education to our products to our raw materials.”
Ogufere emphasised the significance of design in shaping industries and futures, stating that “pretty much everything we see in the world was designed. From the clothes, television, the phone, the floor, everything was designed. And it was designed by people.”
She noted that Africa has been focused on importing goods and ideas that may not be suited to the local context, resulting in a lack of originality and innovation. “We’re almost all down to copying,” Ogufere lamented. “I think, for me, more than anything else, it’s just the amount of activations and the possibilities that we have.”
She highlighted the importance of providing a platform for designers to showcase their work and learn from each other. “We brought in big designers to meet with young designers, to share their experiences and knowledge. We want to create a community that is supportive and innovative.”
The event features various exhibitions, including the Made in Africa exhibition, where designers like T.Y. Bello, Lisa Folawiyo, Juliet Olanipekun amongst others showcase their work.
One of the featured designers, T.Y. Bello, a photographer, debuted her lamp collection at the event. When asked about her inspiration, Bello said, “I’ve always been intrigued by light and I felt like I needed to tell a story. The unknown, the spontaneous, the random, and like what I would call the wind of God and how those things sometimes bring fear and uncertainty but they are the things that actually make our lives beautiful.”
Bello’s work is a reflection of the theme of the event, which celebrates the beauty and creativity of African design. When asked about the theme, Bello said, “I think that the most important thing for me is the inclusivity and understanding that everything has changed, every single thing has changed, nothing remains the same and same goes with design. I love the fact that Titi Ogufere, she’s a disruptor and she’s constantly pushing on those boundaries.”
Ogufere’s vision for Design Week Lagos goes beyond just showcasing design; it’s about creating a movement. “For me, it’s not just an experiment,” she said. “It’s one that we believe will help to develop the industry. It will help to make people see that there are other possibilities and other means of income.” She added that the event aims to promote African creativity and innovation, and to provide a platform for designers to showcase their work.
The Incubator program, which is part of the event, provides training and support to young designers. Ogufere explained that the program was designed to help designers develop their skills and create products that are affordable and relevant to the local market. “We took them through an Incubator program, we made them try to understand our local raw materials. And we said to them, your product must not be more than 250,000 Naira.” The program has already shown promising results, with designers creating innovative products that showcase African creativity.
Ogufere is optimistic about the future of design in Africa, stating that “we’re right in the centre, I would say, of developing what we have inwards.” She added that the event is a testament to the possibilities that exist in Africa, and that design can be a powerful tool for development.
As the event continues, it’s clear that Design Week Lagos is more than just a celebration of design; it’s a movement. It’s a call to action for designers, artists, and creatives to come together and shape the future of Africa. With its focus on innovation, creativity, and inclusivity, Design Week Lagos is set to make a lasting impact on the design industry in Africa

The United States Ambassador to Ghana, Virginia Palmer, has underscored the importance of maintaining a respectful and balanced partnership between Ghana and the United States.
She stressed that despite differences in economic scale and historical timelines, the two nations must continue working together as equals.
“I think we are equals. Your economy is smaller than mine, and you have been independent for less time than the U.S., but I think we must work together as equals. That is number one,” Ambassador Palmer said during an interview on Channel One.
Speaking in an interview on Channel One, she clarified changes regarding the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), noting that its functions would now be overseen by the U.S. State Department.
This transition, she explained, is consistent with her long-standing view that U.S. development assistance, funded by taxpayers, should serve as a foreign policy instrument and be administered accordingly.
“The functions of USAID will now be run by the State Department, by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and that is something, to be honest, I have advocated for decades,” she stated. “I don’t think that will cause any difference in focus or in effect.”
Ambassador Palmer reassured that the U.S. remains firmly committed to its development partnership with Ghana. She emphasised that the change in administrative oversight will not impact the effectiveness or direction of American assistance.
In closing, she reaffirmed Ghana’s continued significance in U.S. foreign policy, highlighting the enduring relationship built on mutual respect and cooperation.

Despite the killing of at least 600 Boko Haram insurgents (JAS and ISWAP) in Borno State in the last three weeks, apprehension remains among the war-weary residents.
The Nigerian military has recorded major successes since revving up its counter-insurgency operation in the North-east, codenamed Operation Hadin Kai.
Those killed by security agencies included at least nine top commanders of the groups terrorising communities in the region by imposing taxes and implementing capital punishments on residents.
PREMIUM TIMES spoke with residents who said the shadows cast by the terrorists in the communities remain despite the intensity and successes of the military operation.
Farmers are still afraid to go to their farms, and the needs for humanitarian assistance continue to rise. In many communities, residents live with the fear of attack when soldiers withdraw after routing the insurgents.
The military renewed its onslaught in the first week of June after the insurgents killed several soldiers and civilians in at least 12 attacks in Borno in the preceding weeks.
At least 94 Insurgents were killed in the first week of June by troops of the Nigerian Army, Multinational Joint Task Force, and the Civilian Joint Task Force (CJTF) in Borno.
However, about 20 security officials also paid the supreme price, including soldiers and members of the CJTF, the local security volunteers supporting the military’s efforts. More than 20 soldiers were also reported wounded.
The insurgents were killed in six encounters in Damboa, Marte, Kumshe (Bama), Bita (Gwoza) and Mairari (Guzamala).
In the Damboa encounter, 16 Insurgents were killed, but a soldier, a CJTF member, and a civilian also died, while about 20 soldiers were reportedly injured after the insurgents attacked the military base in the town.
Zagazola Makama, a security expert, reported that 15 insurgents were killed as soldiers repelled a midnight attack on New Marte. Two soldiers died in the encounter, while eight CJTF members later died in a bomb explosion while searching for the bodies of their comrades on the Dikwa-Marte road.
In Damasak, headquarters of the Mobbar Local Government Area, and the Kumshe area of Bama, troops foiled an early morning attack.
In another encounter in the first week of June, Reuben Kovangiya, an army captain and spokesperson of Operation Hadin Kai, said 60 insurgents were killed when they attacked Bita in Gwoza LGA.
Troops chased the insurgents to their enclaves at Alayani village near Alagarno in the Kukawa LGA with air and ground attacks, killing many, including a high-profile commander, Abu Fatima. Two of his lieutenants, Abu Maryam and Abu Modu, described as IED experts behind attacks that killed several farmers in Kukawa, were also killed.
The last attack recorded in the first week of June was a bomb explosion at a bus stop at Mairari in the Guzamala Local Government Area, in which nine travellers were reportedly killed.
In the second week of June, three prominent Boko Haram/ISWAP leaders, Abu Ali, Ibunu, and Abu Waldume, were killed in Mallam Fatori and Buratai during fierce gun battles. The incident occurred in the early hours of Thursday, 5 June.
On Sallah Day, 6 June, the air component of Operation Hadin Kai bombed a terrorist stronghold at Chiraliya village, near Ajigan in Damboa Local Government Area within the Timbuktu triangle.
The operation, reportedly targeting terrorists preparing for Sallah attacks, resulted in the deaths of over 500 militants, including two prominent Ka’ids (commanders), Abu Dauda and Ya Mohammed, local sources said.
Three days later, on 9 June, soldiers killed more top commanders of the insurgents, including Malam Jidda, who operated in Ngorgore and Malumti villages of Nzalgana, Gujba LGA, and the Tumbuktu Triangle.
Meanwhile, in Abadam, more bodies of terrorists and weapons were recovered during a military operation in Mallamfatori.
However, last week, the insurgents killed 11 people and attacked Gwoza and a Naval base in Kukawa.
The army said some soldiers were wounded in the operation. Mr Reuben said the insurgents had their eyes on the swamped buggies purchased by the Borno State Government for waterways clearance in the Lake Chad region.
The last attack in the week was a bomb explosion that killed 11 people and injured many others in the Konduga LGA.
Communities cry out
Despite the military successes, many Borno residents said they still could not access their farming and fishing areas.
The insurgents were also discouraging businesses with the imposition of illegal taxes.
“Let me reiterate my appeal for the military to take over the entire Guzamala Local Government Area, which has remained under Boko Haram territory, so as to restore civil authority,” the Speaker of the Borno State House of Assembly, Abdulkarim Lawan, said.
Mr Lawson, from Guzamala, described a recent bomb explosion in the town as pathetic. He, however, commended security agencies for the successes recorded so far.
In Kukawa LGA, where many top Boko Haram commanders were killed, residents said they were happy but fear a reprisal attack.
“We heard that the top commanders of Boko Haram who killed our farmers were also killed, and we are happy,” an elderly man in Baga said, commending soldiers for the development.
“We hear gunshots almost every night. But when we see Boko Haram around and we tell soldiers in the town, they would not go,” another resident of Kukawa said.
Residents complained that food was also a problem for them as NGOs’ support had reduced drastically, and the government had been reluctant to support them with food.
“Boko Haram are saying we must register with them before we can farm, and they are killing us. Support from NGOs is also not coming,” a resident said.
In Marte, residents said the attacks happened because security personnel were withdrawn from the town.
“We used to have a Brigade Command but it was moved to Dikwa. Patrolling of the area is poor. But recently, I noticed they brought more soldiers,” Abubakar Hassan, a resident of New Marte, said.
“They (insurgents’) spare women but for men, no matter how small you are, they will just kill you,” he added.
In Gwoza, where the insurgents launched three attacks in four weeks, residents praised the military’s response.
“We are with our soldiers. We are going to fight Boko Haram alongside our troops. This time around, we are not leaving them to destroy our town,” a resident of Gwoza said.
However, in the Wulgo area of Ngala Local Government Area attacked two weeks ago, residents feared another attack after soldiers reportedly withdrew from the area.
“As I am speaking to you, there is no single soldier in Wulgo,” a source in the town who fled to Gamboru Ngala for fear of another attack said.
Governor Babagana Zulum has also celebrated the recent successes of the troops.
The governor mourned the fallen soldiers and volunteers, offering N5 million to each family and a scholarship for their children.
Repentant insurgents returning to the bush
In the last three years, over 300,000 insurgents reportedly repented and were de-radicalised. According to a report by Sahara Reporters, they were subsequently handed over to the Borno State Government.
Some were resettled in their chosen communities, and the others have been enlisted as soldiers to join the fight against their former mates.
According to sources, including prominent Civilian Joint Task Force members, the new soldiers are not trusted.
“To be insincere, I am a Civilian Joint Task Force member but I do not trust them. The military virtually leaves everything in their hands. They tell the military men when, how and where to go.
“Sometimes, if we go to the bush, the repentants will take a different path and won’t come back until after two days. And mind you, when they are going, they will do a lot of shopping, including foodstuffs. Where are they taking all the foodstuffs?”
The source said some have escaped with the new arms, and scores of them wish to return to the bush.
“Some of them are also complaining that the government is not taking care of them; that the promises made to them were not fulfilled. There was also a case of about four of them escaping to the bush with arms and tricycles,” the source added.
PREMIUM TIMES reported how some repentant terrorists escaped in the Konduga-Bama axis, while the International Centre for Investigative Reporting also reported how they were returning to the bush.
FG celebrates troops’ success
Over the last few days, the National Security Adviser, Nuhu Ribadu; the Chief of Defence Staff, Christopher Musa; Chief of Army Staff, Olufemi Oluyede; Chief of Air Staff, Hassan Abubakar, and the Minister of Defence, Abubakar Badaru, said the killings of the insurgents were a significant win in the war against insurgency in the North-east.
The officials urged the troops to sustain the momentum.
Mr Ribadu noted that since President Bola Tinubu assumed office two years ago, over 13,543 Boko Haram elements were killed, while over 11,000 arms were recovered from terrorists.
He said 124,408 Boko Haram fighters and their families surrendered to troops.
The NSA said that despite some setbacks, operations were ongoing in the Timbuktu Triangle, Tumbu islands, and other enclaves to smoke out the insurgents.
Conversely, Amnesty International claimed over 10,000 people have been killed by non-state actors across Nigeria since Mr Tinubu assumed office.
Although the Nigerian government disputes the figure, it has not provided any data to counter it.
Also speaking generally on security, Mr Badaru, the defence minister, said Nigeria was winning the war against terrorism.
About the North-east and North-west regions, the minister said, “Markets are back. Farms are productive again. We have seen Fulani, Hausa, and other communities rebuilding trust. The progress is real and visible.”
However, Abdulsalam Abubakar, an army major-general and Theatre Commander of Operation Hadin Kai, said the infiltration of foreign mercenaries had significantly escalated the threat posed by terrorist groups like Boko Haram and ISWAP.
He revealed the arrest of four Pakistani nationals allegedly involved in arms running for the terrorists.

Par Mamadou SY
Ségou, 18 mai (AMAP) Face à la baisse de la quantité de poissons pêchés dans les lacs, fleuves et barrages, de plus en plus de personnes s’investissent dans la pisciculture afin de répondre à la forte demande des consommateurs. À Ségou, la pisciculture portée par des particuliers connaît un essor prometteur. Levier essentiel de création d’emplois et de développement, ce secteur suscite l’espoir d’une autosuffisance en protéines animales. Cependant, malgré ses atouts, cette activité qui se pratique en milieu naturel ou avec un bassin artificiel se heurte à plusieurs contraintes.
Issu de la toute première promotion de l’Université de Ségou en agroéconomie, Mamoutou dit Djamba Sissoko est le promoteur de «Kanyela-Agri». Cette entreprise évolue dans la pisciculture et le maraîchage depuis 2020. Nous l’avons rencontré en ce mercredi 7 mai en plein travail sur son champ situé au quartier Angoulême. C’est avec beaucoup de passion que Mamoutou Sissoko s’investit dans cette activité rythmée au quotidien par l’alimentation de ses poissons, le contrôle de la qualité de l’eau ainsi que l’entretien des cultures maraîchères. D’un seul bac hors sol au départ, il en compte aujourd’hui 4, grâce au soutien du projet «Jègè ni Jaba» et 2 étangs piscicoles contenant 600 tilapias et 500 clarias.
Le jeune Sissoko met en valeur les déchets organiques produits par les poissons pour fertiliser ses plantes et parvient à tirer son épingle du jeu dans cette activité en générant un chiffre d’affaires d’au moins 500.000 Fcfa avec ses 4 bacs hors sol. Cependant, souligne-t-il, l’envolée des prix des aliments poissons constitue une contrainte majeure pour bon nombre de pisciculteurs. À titre d’illustration, il évoque le sac de 20 kg qui coûte actuellement 28.000 Fcfa contre 16.000 Fca et 40.000 Fcfa pour certaines variétés. Le fondateur de «Kanyela-Agri» estime qu’avec ses 4 bacs hors sol, il doit acheter chaque semaine au moins 20 kg d’aliments pour nourrir ses poissons et cela ne représente que le minimum nécessaire.
Notre jeune entrepreneur déplore le fait que les aliments produits localement ne sont pas suffisamment riches pour permettre une bonne croissance des poissons qui atteignent à peine 700 g en 6 mois. En revanche, dira-t-il, avec des aliments importés, on peut obtenir des poissons de plus de 1 kg en 4 mois. Mamoutou Sissoko lance un appel à l’État et à ses partenaires afin de mettre en place une usine de production d’aliments de poissons de qualité, avant de prôner une meilleure structuration des acteurs concernés et une qualité optimale des intrants subventionnés.
Évoluant dans la production d’alevins et le grossissement de poissons, la ferme piscicole «Kosso» de Madou Diarra (31 ans), propose des services de formation et d’accompagnement aux pisciculteurs. Après l’obtention de son baccalauréat, Madou Diarra réussit le concours d’entrée au Centre de formation pratique en aquaculture de Molodo. Deux ans plus tard, il en sort diplômé en tant qu’agent technique. Après un passage à l’Institut d’économie rurale (IER) de Mopti en tant que superviseur de souches, il décide de lancer sa propre entreprise en 2021.
«Avec la disparition de certaines espèces de poissons, il y a un véritable engouement pour la pisciculture. Nombreuses sont les personnes qui souhaitent se lancer dans ce secteur», note Madou Diarra. Pour les soutenir, une formation sur les fondamentaux de la pisciculture a été développée au sein de sa ferme. Elle attire des participants aux profils variés, avec une forte présence des jeunes.
D’après notre interlocuteur, la pisciculture permet de consommer directement ce que l’on produit, tout en réduisant les importations de poissons. Le responsable de la ferme piscicole «Kosso», souligne qu’avec seulement 300.000 Fcfa, on peut démarrer la pisciculture à petite échelle. Ce budget permet d’acquérir un bac hors sol de 1 m3, 105 alevins, ainsi que plusieurs sacs d’aliments. Madou Diarra déplore le fait que les aliments importés restent coûteux et l’absence de spécialistes qualifiés en pathologie piscicole. À l’avenir, il souhaite que les consommateurs privilégient la production nationale, et que les pisciculteurs puissent répondre à la demande des consommateurs.
Mahamadou Kané, un autre pisciculteur ambitionne de réduire la problématique de l’accès à des intrants piscicoles à travers une production d’alevins de qualité en quantité suffisante et à des prix abordables. L’objectif est de permettre aux acteurs d’accroître leur production. Tirant cette passion de son père, Mahamadou Kané produit aussi des aliments flottants. Avec près de 20 ans d’expériences dans le secteur, la ferme familiale située à Banankoro, s’étend sur 5 hectares. Elle comprend un étang, 16 bassins et une écloserie d’une capacité de production de 100.000 alevins clarias par an. Ce n’est pas tout, le riz est produit sur place, et l’eau provenant de la pisciculture est réutilisée pour irriguer les champs. Des agrumes, melons et pastèques y poussent à profusion.
Même si la pisciculture n’a pas autant de notoriété que l’aviculture, elle reste une activité très lucrative. Mahamadou Kané a révélé qu’en plus de disposer de la souche adéquate, le Mali possède un nombre important d’écloseries pour la production d’alevins, ainsi que des producteurs d’intrants piscicoles et d’aliments pour poissons.
Autant d’atouts que l’État, avec l’appui de ses partenaires, doit saisir pour encourager les citoyens à se tourner vers la pisciculture qui est non seulement une activité rentable, mais aussi un levier de développement.
MS/MD (AMAP)
Baréma Koïta, chef du secteur pêche de Ségou : «Il faut favoriser l’accès aux intrants de qualité à un prix raisonnable»
Par Mamadou SY
Ségou, 18 mai (AMAP) Le service de la pêche a pour rôle l’appui conseil, et le contrôle de la réglementation en vigueur. Selon Baréma Koïta, chef du secteur pêche de Ségou, la pisciculture en tant que technique d’élevage de poisson a vu le jour au Mali par l’initiation d’une petite station piscicole expérimentale dans la Région de San. La convention de financement l’instituant a été signée en novembre 1979 entre le gouvernement de notre pays et celui des États-Unis avec l’appui de l’USAID. C’est ainsi qu’une antenne de vulgarisation a été créée à Niono, dans la zone Office du Niger, en raison de la disponibilité en eau et des sous-produits agroalimentaires. Depuis, une multitude de techniques dont la rizipisciculture et la pisciculture en cage ont été testées et adaptées en milieu rural, a-t-il rappelé.
Concernant les infrastructures piscicoles, le Cercle de Ségou compte actuellement 131 étangs et 115 bacs hors sol et 2 cages flottantes. La rizipisciculture combinant la culture du riz et l’élevage de poissons, couvre une superficie de 7.500 m2, tandis que les mares sont au nombre de 31 et s’étendent sur 51,68 hectares, a détaillé Baréma Koïta. Les performances enregistrées ces dernières années se situent au niveau des cages flottantes et bacs hors sols. Pour une cage flottante de 144 m3 la production obtenue a été de 2.624 kg pour 10.000 alevins. Quant au bac hors sol de 10 m3 avec 1.000 poissons, il a permis de récolter 369 kg, a souligné le chef du secteur pêche de Ségou.
Les tilapias nilotica (Ntèbèfing) et les clarias gariepinus (Manogo) sont les deux espèces ayant fait l’objet d’études positives en ce qui concerne la pisciculture dans notre pays. Parmi les initiatives en cours pour soutenir la pisciculture à Ségou, figurent le Projet de restauration des terres dégradées (PRTD), celui de l’appui à l’amélioration des moyens d’existence durable d’atténuation et d’adaptation des communautés de pêche face aux changements climatiques et Jègè ni Jaba (JNJ), a fait savoir Baréma Koïta.
S’exprimant sur les difficultés, le chef du secteur pêche de Ségou dira que l’acquisition des intrants par les producteurs demeure une préoccupation. En outre, sa structure ne compte pas suffisamment d’agents pour couvrir tout le cercle et l’accès à certaines localités est entravé par l’insécurité grandissante. Le service de la pêche de Ségou fait également face à une insuffisance de moyen financier. Baréma Koïta pense que pour tirer profit de la pisciculture, il faut « favoriser l’accès aux intrants de qualité à un prix raisonnable, disposer d’une source d’eau permanente, suivre régulièrement l’entretien des infrastructures et sécuriser le dispositif contre le vol». Parlant des défis et perspectives, il a évoqué la réduction du coût des intrants, l’aménagement des infrastructures piscicoles et le renforcement des capacités des producteurs.
MS/Md (AMAP)

By Mamadou SY

Segou, 18 May (AMAP) - Faced with the decline in the quantity of fish caught in lakes, rivers and dams, more and more people are investing in fish farming in order to meet strong consumer demand. In Segou, fish farming driven by private individuals is enjoying promising growth. An essential lever for job creation and development, this sector raises hopes of self-sufficiency in animal protein. However, despite its advantages, this activity, which is practised in a natural environment or with an artificial pond, runs up against several constraints.

A member of the very first graduating class of the University of Segou in agro-economics, Mamoutou, known as Djamba Sissoko, is the promoter of "Kanyela-Agri". This business has been operating in fish farming and market gardening since 2020. We met him on Wednesday 7 May, hard at work on his field located in the Angouleme neighbourhood. It is with great passion that Mamoutou Sissoko devotes himself to this activity, whose daily rhythm is set by feeding his fish, checking the water quality and tending his market-garden crops. From a single above-ground tank at the start, he now has 4, thanks to the support of the "Jege ni Jaba" project, and 2 fish ponds containing 600 tilapia and 500 clarias.

The young Sissoko makes use of the organic waste produced by the fish to fertilise his plants and manages to do well in this activity, generating a turnover of at least 500,000 FCFA with his 4 above-ground tanks. However, he stresses, the soaring prices of fish feed are a major constraint for many fish farmers. By way of illustration, he mentions the 20 kg bag which currently costs 28,000 FCFA compared with 16,000 FCFA, and 40,000 FCFA for certain varieties. The founder of "Kanyela-Agri" reckons that with his 4 above-ground tanks he has to buy at least 20 kg of feed every week to feed his fish, and that this represents only the bare minimum required.

Our young entrepreneur deplores the fact that locally produced feeds are not rich enough to allow good growth of the fish, which barely reach 700 g in 6 months. By contrast, he says, with imported feeds one can obtain fish of more than 1 kg in 4 months. Mamoutou Sissoko makes an appeal to the State and its partners to set up a factory producing quality fish feed, and goes on to advocate better structuring of the actors concerned and optimal quality of subsidised inputs.

Working in the production of fingerlings and the growing-on of fish, the "Kosso" fish farm of Madou Diarra (31 years old) offers training and support services to fish farmers. After obtaining his baccalaureate, Madou Diarra passed the entrance examination for the Practical Training Centre in Aquaculture at Molodo. Two years later he graduated as a technical agent. After a spell at the Institute of Rural Economy (IER) in Mopti as a broodstock supervisor, he decided to launch his own business in 2021.

"With the disappearance of certain fish species, there is a real enthusiasm for fish farming. Many people wish to go into this sector," notes Madou Diarra. To support them, a training course on the fundamentals of fish farming has been developed at his farm. It attracts participants with varied profiles, with a strong presence of young people.

According to our interviewee, fish farming makes it possible to consume directly what one produces, while reducing fish imports. The head of the "Kosso" fish farm stresses that with only 300,000 FCFA one can start fish farming on a small scale. This budget makes it possible to acquire a 1 m3 above-ground tank, 105 fingerlings, as well as several bags of feed. Madou Diarra deplores the fact that imported feeds remain costly and the absence of qualified specialists in fish pathology. In the future, he would like consumers to favour national production, and fish farmers to be able to meet consumer demand.

Mahamadou Kane, another fish farmer, aims to reduce the problem of access to fish-farming inputs through the production of quality fingerlings in sufficient quantity and at affordable prices. The objective is to enable the actors to increase their production. Having inherited this passion from his father, Mahamadou Kane also produces floating feeds. With nearly 20 years of experience in the sector, the family farm located at Banankoro extends over 5 hectares. It comprises one pond, 16 basins and a hatchery with a production capacity of 100,000 clarias fingerlings per year. That is not all: rice is produced on site, and the water coming from the fish farming is reused to irrigate the fields. Citrus fruits, melons and watermelons grow there in abundance.

Even if fish farming does not have as much renown as poultry farming, it remains a very lucrative activity. Mahamadou Kane revealed that, in addition to having the appropriate broodstock, Mali possesses a significant number of hatcheries for the production of fingerlings, as well as producers of fish-farming inputs and fish feed.

So many assets that the State, with the support of its partners, must seize in order to encourage citizens to turn to fish farming, which is not only a profitable activity but also a lever of development.

MS/MD (AMAP)

Barema Koita, head of the fisheries sector of Segou: "Access to quality inputs at a reasonable price must be facilitated"

By Mamadou SY

Segou, 18 May (AMAP) - The fisheries service has the role of advisory support and the monitoring of the regulations in force. According to Barema Koita, head of the fisheries sector of Segou, fish farming as a fish-rearing technique came into being in Mali with the establishment of a small experimental fish-farming station in the Region of San. The financing agreement instituting it was signed in November 1979 between the government of our country and that of the United States with the support of USAID. Thus an extension outpost was created at Niono, in the Office du Niger zone, because of the availability of water and of agri-food by-products. Since then, a multitude of techniques including rice-fish farming and cage fish farming have been tested and adapted in rural areas, he recalled.

Concerning fish-farming infrastructure, the Cercle of Segou currently counts 131 ponds and 115 above-ground tanks and 2 floating cages. Rice-fish farming, combining rice cultivation and fish rearing, covers an area of 7,500 m2, while the ponds number 31 and extend over 51.68 hectares, Barema Koita detailed. The performances recorded in recent years are at the level of floating cages and above-ground tanks. For a floating cage of 144 m3 the production obtained was 2,624 kg for 10,000 fingerlings. As for the above-ground tank of 10 m3 with 1,000 fish, it made it possible to harvest 369 kg, the head of the fisheries sector of Segou stressed.

Tilapia nilotica (Ntebefing) and Clarias gariepinus (Manogo) are the two species which have been the subject of positive studies as regards fish farming in our country. Among the initiatives under way to support fish farming in Segou are the Degraded Land Restoration Project (PRTD), the project to support the improvement of sustainable livelihoods, mitigation and adaptation of fishing communities in the face of climate change, and Jege ni Jaba (JNJ), Barema Koita reported.

Speaking on the difficulties, the head of the fisheries sector of Segou said that the acquisition of inputs by producers remains a concern. In addition, his structure does not have enough agents to cover the whole cercle and access to certain localities is hampered by growing insecurity. The fisheries service of Segou also faces insufficient financial means. Barema Koita thinks that in order to benefit from fish farming it is necessary to "facilitate access to quality inputs at a reasonable price, have a permanent water source, regularly monitor the maintenance of the infrastructure and secure the facilities against theft". Speaking of challenges and prospects, he mentioned reducing the cost of inputs, the development of fish-farming infrastructure and capacity-building for producers.

MS/Md (AMAP)

a4325.t:
Le Soudan, en proie à une guerre dévastatrice depuis près de deux ans, fait face à une crise humanitaire d’une ampleur inédite, la vie dans le pays étant devenue un « véritable enfer », selon une haute responsable onusienne.
Plus de 12 millions de personnes ont été déplacées à l’intérieur du pays et à l’extérieur, et plus de 24 millions de Soudanais souffrent de faim aiguë, a alerté mercredi la directrice des opérations et de la communication de l’OCHA (Bureau de coordination des affaires humanitaires de lONU), Edem Wosornu, lors d’une réunion du Conseil de sécurité de l’ONU. « Le conflit ininterrompu au Soudan a infligé des souffrances immenses et transformé certaines parties du pays en véritable enfer », a-t-elle déploré.
Depuis avril 2023, ce pays d’Afrique de l’est est le théâtre d’un conflit opposant l’armée du général Abdel Fattah al-Burhane aux paramilitaires des Forces de soutien rapide (FSR), après le coup d’État d’octobre 2021. Cette guerre a non seulement ravagé les infrastructures, mais elle a aussi détruit les services essentiels, notamment les systèmes de santé et d’éducation. Le Soudan est désormais aux prises avec un effondrement total des services, un nombre croissant de violences sexuelles et des millions d’enfants traumatisés.
Un des points névralgiques de la crise se trouve dans le camp de réfugiés de Zamzam, situé dans le Darfour du Nord, où les combats se sont récemment intensifiés, détruisant des installations vitales, notamment les marchés. Ce camp fait partie des zones où la famine a été officiellement déclarée depuis août 2023. Le Programme alimentaire mondial (PAM) et Médecins sans frontières (MSF), principaux fournisseurs d’aide humanitaire, ont dû suspendre leurs activités en raison de la violence croissante.
La situation se dégrade également à Khartoum, la capitale, où des exécutions sommaires et des violences ciblent la population civile. Dans le sud du pays, les combats s’étendent au Kordofan du Nord et Sud, affectant gravement les civils et l’accès humanitaire. Des rapports ont aussi fait état de nouvelles atrocités dans l’Etat du Nil Blanc, avec des dizaines de civils tués lors d’attaques début février.
Face à cette crise, la communauté internationale a lancé un appel de fonds de 6 milliards de dollars pour 2025 afin de soutenir la réponse humanitaire. Ces fonds permettront d’aider 21 millions de Soudanais à l’intérieur du pays et cinq millions de réfugiés dans les pays voisins. Cependant, la situation demeure critique, l’acheminement de l’aide étant entravé par l’insécurité, la bureaucratie et l’ingérence des parties en conflit.
ODL/Sf/ac/APA
a4325.en:
Sudan, gripped by a devastating war for nearly two years, is facing a humanitarian crisis of unprecedented scale, with life in the country having become a “veritable hell”, according to a senior UN official.

More than 12 million people have been displaced inside and outside the country, and more than 24 million Sudanese are suffering acute hunger, warned the Director of Operations and Communication of OCHA (the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs), Edem Wosornu, on Wednesday at a meeting of the UN Security Council. “The uninterrupted conflict in Sudan has inflicted immense suffering and turned parts of the country into a veritable hell,” she deplored.

Since April 2023, this East African country has been the theatre of a conflict pitting the army of General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan against the paramilitaries of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), following the coup d’état of October 2021. This war has not only devastated infrastructure, it has also destroyed essential services, notably the health and education systems. Sudan is now grappling with a total collapse of services, a growing number of cases of sexual violence and millions of traumatised children.

One of the nerve centres of the crisis is in the Zamzam refugee camp, located in North Darfur, where fighting has recently intensified, destroying vital facilities, notably markets. This camp is among the areas where famine has been officially declared since August 2023. The World Food Programme (WFP) and Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), the main providers of humanitarian aid, have had to suspend their activities because of the growing violence.

The situation is also deteriorating in Khartoum, the capital, where summary executions and violence target the civilian population. In the south of the country, fighting is spreading to North and South Kordofan, seriously affecting civilians and humanitarian access. Reports have also described new atrocities in White Nile State, with dozens of civilians killed in attacks in early February.

Faced with this crisis, the international community has launched a funding appeal of 6 billion dollars for 2025 to support the humanitarian response. These funds will make it possible to help 21 million Sudanese inside the country and five million refugees in neighbouring countries. However, the situation remains critical, with the delivery of aid hampered by insecurity, bureaucracy and interference from the parties to the conflict.

ODL/Sf/ac/APA

La Nation Bénin...
Le Conseil d’administration du Millennium Challenge Account (MCA-Bénin II) a tenu, jeudi 29 septembre à Cotonou, sa quatrième session ordinaire. Il y est annoncé l’entrée en vigueur du programme pour le premier trimestre 2017.
Les préparatifs pour le démarrage effectif des projets du deuxième compact du Millennium Challenge Account (MCA-Bénin II) amorcent la dernière ligne droite. L’entrée en vigueur du programme est attendue pour le premier trimestre 2017, selon les projections de Samuel Batcho, coordonnateur national de MCA-Bénin II. La 4è session ordinaire du Conseil d’administration de l’institution tenue, jeudi 29 septembre à Cotonou, a connu des dossiers dont l’adoption devrait permettre de franchir un pas de plus vers le lancement des divers chantiers du deuxième compact. A l’ordre du jour, il était retenu, entre autres, l’étude et l’approbation de plusieurs documents de décaissement de fonds, au titre du dernier trimestre de l’année en cours. « Depuis la dernière session, nous avons poursuivi le processus de mise en place du personnel et du cadre de travail. Une première vague du personnel est déjà installée. Le traitement des dossiers de la seconde vague est en cours. Nous estimons qu’à fin octobre prochain, le personnel sera au complet», souligne le coordonnateur national. L’équipe déjà en place, a aussi travaillé à la finalisation de l’évaluation d’offres de marché et de cotations diverses.
«Ce programme nous est important parce qu’il nous permettra de lever les contraintes liées à la disponibilité de l’énergie électrique dans notre pays. La levée de ces obstacles est un facteur essentiel pour booster la croissance économique», précise Abdoulaye Bio Tchané, ministre d’Etat en charge du Développement, président du Conseil d’administration de MCA-Bénin II. Il rassure que la 4e session du Conseil d’administration va sortir des résolutions qui marqueront la détermination des administrateurs d’aller vite vers la mise en vigueur.
Le second compact du MCA mobilise en faveur du Bénin environ 403 millions de dollars, soit plus de 200 milliards de francs CFA sur cinq ans, dont 28 millions de dollars (environ 14 milliards) de contribution nationale. Ce nouvel appui américain, exclusivement dédié au secteur énergétique, a pour objectif, l’amélioration du cadre institutionnel et juridique et la réalisation des investissements durables dans le secteur énergétique. Sa signature a eu lieu le 9 septembre 2015 à Washington aux Etats-Unis.

La Nation Benin...

The Board of Directors of the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA-Benin II) held its fourth ordinary session in Cotonou on Thursday 29 September. The programme’s entry into force was announced there for the first quarter of 2017.

Preparations for the effective start-up of the projects of the second Millennium Challenge Account compact (MCA-Benin II) are entering the home stretch. The programme’s entry into force is expected in the first quarter of 2017, according to the projections of Samuel Batcho, national coordinator of MCA-Benin II. The 4th ordinary session of the institution’s Board of Directors, held on Thursday 29 September in Cotonou, took up files whose adoption should make it possible to take a further step toward the launch of the various worksites of the second compact. On the agenda were, among other items, the review and approval of several fund disbursement documents for the last quarter of the current year. “Since the last session, we have continued the process of putting the staff and the working framework in place. A first wave of staff is already installed. The processing of the second wave’s files is under way. We estimate that by the end of next October the staff will be complete,” the national coordinator stressed. The team already in place has also worked on finalising the evaluation of procurement bids and various quotations.

“This programme is important to us because it will allow us to lift the constraints linked to the availability of electrical energy in our country. Lifting these obstacles is an essential factor for boosting economic growth,” said Abdoulaye Bio Tchané, Minister of State in charge of Development and chairman of the Board of Directors of MCA-Benin II. He gave assurances that the 4th session of the Board of Directors would produce resolutions marking the directors’ determination to move quickly toward entry into force.

The second MCA compact mobilises for Benin about 403 million dollars, that is more than 200 billion CFA francs over five years, of which 28 million dollars (about 14 billion) is a national contribution. This new American support, devoted exclusively to the energy sector, aims to improve the institutional and legal framework and to carry out sustainable investments in the energy sector. It was signed on 9 September 2015 in Washington, in the United States.

a4851.t:
The title of this article draws inspiration from a statement made by the United States Treasury Secretary, Mr. Scott Bessent, during his address to corporate America. His remarks sought to clarify President Donald Trump’s sweeping economic measures—policies now widely referred to as Trump’s “tariff war.”
In an interesting twist, Bessent has emerged as the “good cop” in the Trump administration’s policy rollout. While President Trump is often portrayed by his critics as the “bad cop,” Bessent has been the one softening the edges of Trump’s hardline trade and foreign policy stance, explaining them in a friendlier and more accessible way. This “good cop, bad cop” dynamic has become a key communication strategy for an administration that is disrupting the old world trade order and reshaping it into a new one—one driven by tariffs and economic leverage that has put 192 of the world’s 193 nations on alert.
Yet, alongside the controversy, Trump is increasingly proving himself to be one of America’s most remarkable salesmen—and perhaps even a statesman—sealing high-value deals not only with corporations but also with sovereign nations. This should not come as a surprise. After all, Trump co-authored the 1987 bestseller The Art of the Deal with Tony Schwartz, a book that has become a classic on salesmanship and negotiation.
What’s notable in Trump’s second term—since his return to the presidency on January 20—is how he has elevated tariffs from being merely an economic tool to becoming a security instrument. True to his pledge to end wars rather than start them, Trump has played active roles in brokering ceasefires in conflicts such as India–Pakistan and the Democratic Republic of Congo–Rwanda (via the M23 militia).
So impactful have these interventions been that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu recently recommended Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize, crediting him for efforts to end the Israel–Gaza war. Netanyahu formally submitted a nomination letter to the Nobel Committee in the Oval Office, praising Trump’s peacemaking initiatives.
Israel is not alone in this push. Cambodia’s Prime Minister Hun Manet has also nominated Trump for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, citing his role in halting armed conflict between Cambodia and Thailand after a territorial dispute displaced over 300,000 people. According to both countries’ leaders, a phone call from Trump on July 26 broke the deadlock, leading to a Malaysia-brokered ceasefire on July 28. In its letter to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, Cambodia praised Trump’s “extraordinary statesmanship” and “visionary diplomacy,” noting that his intervention prevented a potentially catastrophic war.
Adding to this growing list, Azerbaijan and Armenia have jointly nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize. Their nations have been locked in a century-long conflict that traces back to oil interests in the Baku region in the early 20th century. Historical accounts suggest that Western oil magnates—the Rockefellers and Rothschilds—sought to secure their refining operations by involving the Turkish army in what became the Armenian genocide of 1915. The violence predated the Holocaust and has fueled sporadic hostilities for over a hundred years.
That is why the recent peace deal—signed at the White House and mediated by Trump—is so historic. Both President Ilham Aliyev of Azerbaijan and Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan of Armenia credited Trump’s diplomacy for achieving this breakthrough. Aliyev stated, “Who, if not President Trump, deserves a Nobel Peace Prize?” while Pashinyan echoed, “He has earned it.”
Pakistan, as earlier noted, is also among the nations nominating Trump. Its nomination is based on his role in ending a recent flare-up with India over the disputed Kashmir region. In April this year, a four-day war erupted after militants killed 25 Indian tourists in Kashmir. With tensions escalating between these two nuclear powers—nations that were one country until their religiously based partition in 1947—Trump stepped in, threatening both with higher tariffs if they did not cease hostilities. The pressure worked, averting a potential nuclear confrontation.
Through these examples, Trump is demonstrating that “America First” does not mean “America Alone.” Instead, he is leveraging America’s economic power to reinforce global stability—proving that tariffs can be as potent a tool for peace as they are for trade.
Another significant development in the wave of nominations for President Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize is the joint endorsement by Azerbaijan and Armenia. This marks a major milestone in the apparent global groundswell for Trump’s recognition as a peacemaker, underscored by his active role in ending conflicts across the world.
In light of this scenario—where at least half a dozen nations are nominating President Trump as a candidate for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for Peace—it is worth noting that, although Trump’s campaign mantra is America First, he has not only successfully pushed that agenda by making the U.S. less of a “Santa Claus” through measures such as suspending USAID (a platform through which America engages in global philanthropy), he has also maintained a sharp focus on keeping the world free of wars through mediation efforts.
This is evident in his involvement in attempts to end the Russia–Ukraine war, now in its third year, as well as the Israeli–Gaza conflict, which is nearing its second year. To pursue global peace—which skeptics worldwide often deem impossible—President Trump has even taken the unprecedented step of sanctioning India by imposing a 50% trade tariff for breaching the global sanctions against Russia by purchasing its oil. It is worth noting that China also buys oil from Russia. However, while China is not currently facing the same high tariff as India, it has been engaged in negotiations with the U.S. after being hit with a record 145% tariff during their trade face-off earlier in April.
That hefty tariff was part of Trump’s reciprocal trade policy, which saw him impose duties as high as 145% on Chinese goods, while offering a 90-day pause (starting April 2) to friendly nations that were in the process of adjusting their tariffs on U.S. imports. Interestingly, the pause period—originally due to end on July 9—was extended first to August 1, and then again to August 12, which expires today, Tuesday, August 12.
In the interim, the tariff on China was revised downwards after several rounds of meetings between the world’s two largest economies in Switzerland. The double extension of tariff implementation for over 90 countries reflects Trump’s open-door policy, showing that America First does not mean America Alone. He appears willing to adjust timelines rather than being rigid in enforcement.
While critics mock this approach by labeling it “TACO”—short for “Trump Always Chickens Out,” a wordplay on taco, the popular Mexican dish—they overlook the negotiation tactic behind it. The TACO nickname pokes fun at Trump’s willingness to give trading partners more time rather than enforcing stiff, unmovable deadlines. However, from a negotiation standpoint, this flexibility allows partners to conduct the necessary consultations to reach mutually beneficial agreements.
Trump’s view is that the new tariffs are fundamentally reciprocal, designed to end unfair trade practices against the U.S. The point of introducing new rules and deadlines, he argues, is to secure compliance—not to punish unnecessarily. Without adequate time for adjustment, compliance becomes less likely. As the classic negotiation principle goes, a win–win outcome is ideal: one that meets the needs of all parties. This principle—outlined in Roger Fisher and William Ury’s seminal book Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In— emphasizes that a good agreement leaves no party feeling cheated.
Beyond tariffs, Trump has also issued deadlines for Iran to negotiate an end to its suspected nuclear enrichment program, warning of dire consequences. When Iran failed to comply, the U.S. bombed its known nuclear facilities with B-22 bombers equipped with bunker-buster bombs that had never before been used.
Just last week, President Trump issued Russia an ultimatum to end its more than three-year war against Ukraine. This came after Russia launched a massive bombardment of Ukraine, drawing criticism that Trump was not being tough enough despite earlier sanctions. The Trump administration had also facilitated meetings between Russia and Ukraine in Turkey to negotiate peace, but these failed, allegedly because Russia did not send senior officials or honor the agreed terms.
Rather than enforcing deadlines rigidly, Trump has opted for flexibility—extending tariff deadlines for countries worldwide and adopting the same approach for the Russian–Ukrainian and Israeli– Hamas conflicts, both of which are taking a devastating toll on the global economy.
Trump’s focus on ending these wars is driven not only by humanitarian concerns but also by the fact that both regions are critical suppliers of two essential resources—grains and fossil fuels. These commodities are the lifeblood of the global economy and the foundation of human survival on earth.
As we all know, Russia and Ukraine are the largest global sources of wheat and other grains, just as the Middle East is the hub of fossil fuel production and therefore the world’s primary energy source. Leading economists have acknowledged that shortages in the free flow of both commodities are largely responsible for the significant slowdown in the global economy, triggering the current hardships gripping humanity.
Without a doubt, the continued wars in these critical regions over the past three years have severely affected the world’s economy, justifying President Trump’s desire to end them—using both military means (arming Israel and Ukraine) and economic tools (imposing sanctions on Russia).
In my view, these moves are evidence of the America First, not America Alone policy, as Trump has sought to end the Israel–Hamas and Russia– Ukraine wars to achieve global peace for the socio-economic prosperity of humanity.
Currently, a new deadline has been set by the Trump administration for Russia—a fellow nuclear power—to end the war. In response, former President Dmitry Medvedev, now in charge of Russia’s war arsenal, has appeared to issue a veiled threat to the U.S. But Russia has stepped back from its initial hard stance by accepting to negotiate an end to its siege on Ukraine.
A similar ultimatum was issued to end the Israel–Hamas war. It was ignored, and the conflict has escalated, causing a horrific humanitarian crisis in Gaza. The world watches in shock as civilians face severe hunger, compounded by the devastation of ongoing bombardments that began in October 2020.
Only last week, President Trump called on Hamas to release the hostages taken during its 2023 incursion into Israel so that the Israeli siege on Palestine could end. Meanwhile, against the backdrop of the ongoing food blockade into Palestine—which is resulting in mass starvation—France and the UK, alongside Canada (the latest to join), have announced they will recognize Palestine as a nation. This development marks a departure from the traditional Western stance of withholding recognition.

SpaceX and Tesla boss Musk is presiding over a purge of US government jobs that critics call an ‘evisceration of democracy’.
US President Donald Trump has said he expects his ally Elon Musk to find billions of dollars of fraud and abuse at the Pentagon, after he was tasked with leading an audit to slash the size of the US federal workforce.
“We’re going to find billions, hundreds of millions of dollars of fraud and abuse,” Trump said of the largest federal department in an interview with Fox News, an excerpt of which was aired on Sunday morning.

“And, you know, the people elected me on that.”
The Pentagon’s budget is approaching $1 trillion per year. In December, then-President Joe Biden signed a bill authorising $895bn in defence spending for the fiscal year ending on September 30.
Right-wing billionaire and SpaceX and Tesla boss Musk, who the White House appointed to head the newly-created Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), will have access to confidential information in computer systems at various government agencies in order to fulfil the set task.
Leaders from across the political spectrum have long criticised waste and inefficiency at the Pentagon, but critics say these efforts risk exposing classified information and gutting entire agencies without congressional approval.
Musk’s companies also hold major contracts with the Pentagon, which has raised significant conflict-of-interest concerns. A US judge on Saturday issued an emergency order blocking DOGE from accessing Treasury Department payment systems that contain Americans’ sensitive data.
Despite the concerns, Trump seemed to double down on the idea, saying he was going to ask Musk “very soon, like maybe in 24 hours, to go check the Department of Education. … Then I’m going to go, go to the military”.
National Security Advisor Mike Waltz suggested in a separate interview on Sunday that the Pentagon’s shipbuilding processes could be an area of particular interest.
“Everything there seems to cost too much, take too long and deliver too little to the soldiers… We do need business leaders to go in there and absolutely reform the Pentagon’s acquisition process,” Waltz said in an interview with NBC News.
Over his three weeks in office, Trump has issued a flurry of executive orders aimed at slashing federal spending – including halting funds to the US Agency for International Development (USAID) – but evidence of widespread fraud has not been presented.
On Saturday, the Trump administration ordered the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to stop nearly all its work, effectively shutting down an agency that was created to protect consumers after the 2008 financial crisis and subprime mortgage-lending scandal.
Democrats have slammed Trump’s efforts. Senator Chris Murphy on Sunday warned of an “assault on the Constitution” and said Trump was ushering in a “billionaire takeover of government”.
“The president wants to be able to decide how and where money is spent so that he can reward his political friends, he can punish his political enemies,” Murphy told ABC News. “That is the evisceration of democracy.”
Source: Al Jazeera and news agencies

Minister of Water and Sanitation Abida Mia has urged the tea sector to embrace value-addition for the country to reap more benefits.
She made the remarks on Thursday at the Malawi Tea Tasting Event at the House of Commons in the United Kingdom (UK).
The event, which drew officials from the UK and Malawi tea sectors, including UK members of Parliament (MPs), was organised to showcase Malawi’s tea.
“While we take pride in Malawi’s rich tea history, the future demands that we evolve. It is time to focus on value-addi tion—moving
beyond simply producing raw tea and investing in processes such as blending, packaging, and branding within Malawi itself,” said Mia.
She also called for collaboration among tea sector players to propel Malawi tea onto the global stage.
Said Mia: “Together we can invest in both branding and value-added processes that can propel Malawian tea onto the global stage.”
Tea Association of Malawi chairperson Sangwani Hara said his association believes that trade pacts and enhanced trade can provide a good alternative to aid and development assistance.
He said: “With increased tea imports from Malawi, British tea drinkers will be allowed to consume a great product at a fair price while contributing to Malawi’s and tea estates’ foreign exchange earnings and development agenda.”
In his remarks, Malawi High Commissioner Thomas Bisika, who mooted the idea of the Malawi Tea Tasting Event, said tea will play a significant role as Malawi transitions from aid to trade.
He thanked Sureena Brackenridge, MP, and Warinder Juss, MP, for hosting the event.
On his part, London Tea Exchange chief executive officer Sheikh Aliur Rahman called for fair play in the tea production chain.
Tea is one of Malawi’s foreign exchange earners, contributing about eight percent to forex earnings, and 11 percent to national employment.
The local tea industry employs over 60 000 temporary and permanent workers.

a4998.t:
Malawi has recorded three new cases of Mpox, bringing the number of recorded infections to 15 since the outbreak was declared on April 16 2025.
The new cases, according to the daily update released on Thursday by the Public Health Institute of Malawi (Phim), have pushed the number of affected districts to three; all of which have reported cases within the past 42 days.
Malawi is one of 16 countries in Africa reporting Mpox outbreaks as health officials battle with vaccine shortages as well as limited testing and hospital capacity.
Recently, the Phim suggested that a majority of the patients were aged between 17 and 41.
“Investigations are underway to establish the possible source of infection and trace contacts,” the institute said in a statement last week.
Meanwhile, a report this week in the UK’s The Guardian newspaper quoted Lilongwe district health office spokesperson, Richard Mvula, as saying: “A commonality about these cases is that some were immune-compromised.”
According to the report, patients who were on antiretroviral therapy (ART) had been forced to stop taking their medication because of drug shortages.
HIV can worsen the risk and severity of Mpox, while effective HIV treatment can help manage the risk and people living with HIV, especially those with uncontrolled viral loads, may experience a more severe form of Mpox.
The surge in Mpox cases follows US government aid cuts to healthcare, including HIV programmes that have badly hit the country and raised fears of an escalation of infectious diseases.
However, despite the continued rise in infections, no deaths have been reported so far, maintaining the Mpox case fatality rate at 0.0 percent.
According to the update, only one patient is currently admitted to a treatment facility, while no new discharges have been registered in the latest notice.
Reacting to the surge in cases, Malawi Health Equity Network (Mhen) executive director, George Jobe, described the situation as worrisome and stressed the need for all stakeholders to engage an extra gear to curb the viral infection.
“For instance, we should analyse if there are similarities in the people who are testing positive, such as economic status, social status, urban versus rural among other parameters. This will help to determine if the surge is as a result of limited knowledge among the public or other things,” Jobe said.
He also highlighted the need to publicise the numbers of cases in the media so that people are reminded about the problem amidst us.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Health has reiterated its call for vigilance and early reporting of symptoms as part of efforts to contain the spread of the virus.

a5089.t:
La Tunisie a reçu dimanche un groupe de ses citoyens, passagers de la flottille Global Sumud (GSF) libérés après avoir été illégalement arrêtés par Israël alors qu’ils voulaient rompre le blocus imposé à Gaza.
La flottille Global Sumud était partie de Barcelone (Espagne) au début du mois de septembre avec pour objectif de rompre le blocus imposé par Israël à la bande de Gaza, et de livrer de l’aide humanitaire au territoire palestinien. Mais, elle a été interceptée la semaine dernière par la marine israélienne.
Neuf membres tunisiens de la flottille sont rentrés en Tunisie dimanche après avoir été relâchés par les autorités israéliennes, selon la presse locale.
Le groupe a atterri à l’aéroport international de Tunis-Carthage en provenance la Turkiye après trois jours de détention en Israël.
Ils ont été accueillis par des centaines de personnes, dont des membres de leurs familles, des journalistes et des représentants de la société civile, selon les médias tunisiens.
Parmi les participants figuraient Aziz Meliani, Noureddine Slaouej, Abdallah Messaoudi, Housemeddine Remadi, Zied Jaballah, Hamza Bouzouida, Mohamed Mrad, Anis Abbassi et Lotfi Hajji. Un autre Tunisien, Mohamed Ali Mohieddine, capitaine du navire Amsterdam, était rentré plus tôt le même jour.
Au moins 15 bateaux de la flottille Soumoud ont été illégalement interceptés par les forces israéliennes dans les eaux internationales.
Au départ, les passagers de ces bateaux avaient été conduits vers des ports israéliens, puis placés en détention avant d’être expulsés vers leurs pays d’origine. Certains sont toujours détenus par Israël.
AK/ac/Sf/APA
a5089.en:
Return of the Tunisians from the flotilla intercepted by Israel

Tunisia on Sunday received a group of its citizens, passengers of the Global Sumud Flotilla (GSF), released after having been illegally arrested by Israel as they sought to break the blockade imposed on Gaza.

The Global Sumud flotilla had set out from Barcelona (Spain) at the beginning of September with the aim of breaking the blockade imposed by Israel on the Gaza Strip and delivering humanitarian aid to the Palestinian territory. But it was intercepted last week by the Israeli navy.

Nine Tunisian members of the flotilla returned to Tunisia on Sunday after being released by the Israeli authorities, according to the local press.

The group landed at Tunis-Carthage International Airport, arriving from Türkiye, after three days of detention in Israel.

They were welcomed by hundreds of people, including members of their families, journalists and representatives of civil society, according to Tunisian media.

Among the participants were Aziz Meliani, Noureddine Slaouej, Abdallah Messaoudi, Housemeddine Remadi, Zied Jaballah, Hamza Bouzouida, Mohamed Mrad, Anis Abbassi and Lotfi Hajji. Another Tunisian, Mohamed Ali Mohieddine, captain of the ship Amsterdam, had returned earlier the same day.

At least 15 boats of the Soumoud flotilla were illegally intercepted by Israeli forces in international waters.

Initially, the passengers of these boats were taken to Israeli ports, then placed in detention before being expelled to their countries of origin. Some are still detained by Israel.

AK/ac/Sf/APA

a5162.t:
African Mining Week will connect global investors with investment and project opportunities in Zambia – home to significant critical mineral reserves
CAPE TOWN, South Africa, August 6, 2025/ — Zambia’s Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development has outlined the vast critical mineral opportunities available across the country in a report released in collaboration with the British Geological Survey. Covering strategic minerals such as copper, cobalt, manganese and more, the report underscores the instrumental role the country already plays in global supply chains.
The report comes ahead of African Mining Week (AMW) – Africa’s premier gathering for mining stakeholders. Taking place October 1-3 in Cape Town, the event will feature a dedicated panel on Zambia, titled Zambia: Accelerating Exploration and Development Through License Allocation. The session will unpack the country’s strategy to unlock its full mineral potential, outlining investment prospects, market trends and partnership opportunities.
Copper
As the tenth-largest copper producer globally – contributing 3% of total output – Zambia is expected to play a critical role in meeting the anticipated rise in global demand – projected to increase 25% by 2040. With several large-scale projects set to come online by 2026, including Sinomine Resources’ Kitumba Mine, Mimosa Resources’ Kashime Mine and KoBold Metals’ Mingomba Mine, Zambia’s copper sector is primed for expansion. The country has set a target to increase production to three million tons by 2031, highlighting a unique opportunity for mining firms.
Cobalt
In 2024, six operations in Zambia were actively producing cobalt from copper. Together with the Democratic Republic of Congo, Zambia holds 58% of the world’s cobalt-bearing copper resources. The commissioning of Africa’s first cobalt sulfate refinery by the end of 2025 in Zambia will expand the country’s cobalt output. The project is led by Kobaloni Energy and backed by a $100 million investment from Vision Blue and the Africa Finance Corporation. U.S.-based Terra Metals is also relaunching a copper-cobalt acid leach plant in the Kabompo Dome area in 2025.
Manganese
Zambia’s Luapula Province is the country’s manganese hub. Musamu Resources’ Luongo Open-Pit Mine – Zambia’s first large-scale manganese mine – began operations in 2022 and aims to scale output to one million tons per year by 2027. Kabundi Resources also operates two washing plants in Serenje.
Nickel
Zambia hosts two nickel operations: the Enterprise Project owned by First Quantum Minerals and the Munali Mine operated by Mabiza Resources. Annual production rose from 2,500 tons in 2019 to 8,000 tons in 2023, with global demand expected to climb by 70% by 2040.
Graphite
Significant graphite prospects have been identified in Petauke, Lundazi and Kapiri Mposhi, with high-grade discoveries at the Mvuvye and Njoka sites. Other known discoveries include the Sasare and Mkonda deposits. As companies such as Malaika Exploration move to commercialize these assets, Zambia is set to contribute to meeting a forecast 130% surge in global graphite demand by 2040, driven by growth in the electric vehicle sector.
Lithium
Zambia’s lithium potential is concentrated in the Choma Belt of the Southern Province. UK-based First Africa Metals has confirmed high-grade deposits at its Misika and Kandela projects, with additional exploration ongoing across Tonga, Konayuma and Rock Valley. With global lithium demand set to grow by 350% by 2040, these assets could significantly boost Zambia’s export revenues and job creation.
Rare Earth Elements
With global Rare Earth Element demand forecast to rise by 65% by 2040, Zambia is ramping up exploration. Antler Gold is progressing at its Kesya Project, while x-RAM Traws is advancing the Nkombwa Hill discovery.
Columbite-Tantalite
Columbite-tantalite – critical in electronics, aerospace and energy – represents an untapped opportunity for Zambia to diversify its mineral base and revenue streams. Exploration is underway by Maamba Collieries in the Southern Province and Malaika Exploration in north-eastern Zambia. With global demand for the mineral projected to increase by up to 525% by 2040, Zambia’s reserves are becoming increasingly strategic in global supply chains.
Distributed by APO Group on behalf of Energy Capital & Power.
