Le ministre en charge de l’Economie maritime, Patrick Yérima a effectué hier mardi 4 août, une descente au Port autonome de Cotonou (PAC) et sur les installations de la Société béninoise de manutention portuaire (SOBEMAP). Objectif, toucher du doigt les problèmes auxquels sont confrontés les employés et usagers de ces sociétés sous tutelle de son département ministériel.
Patrick Yérima a pris les rênes du ministère de l’Economie maritime et des Infrastructures portuaires, il y a quelques semaines à la faveur du dernier remaniement ministériel. C’est pour avoir une vue plus large des activités menées par les structures sous sa tutelle qu’il a effectué hier mardi 4 août le tour des services stratégiques du Port autonome de Cotonou et de la Société béninoise de manutention portuaire (SOBEMAP).
A sa descente dans l’enceinte du Port autonome de Cotonou, le ministre Patrick Yérima a eu une séance de travail avec le directeur général du PAC, Samuel Batcho et celui de la Sobemap, Antoine Kouton, avant de visiter les infrastructures portuaires. 
Le directeur général de la SOBEMAP, lui a fait une brève description du fonctionnement des machines utilisées dans le cadre des chargements et déchargements des conteneurs. Les engins de diverses marques occupent des dizaines de mètres sur le domaine de la société. Antoine Kouton a expliqué au ministre, les difficultés auxquelles fait face sa société. Parfois les pièces des engins tombent en panne en pleine opération et leurs pièces de rechange nécessitent l’observance stricte des règles prescrites par le Code des marchés publics qui interdit les passations gré à gré. «S’il y a 2 ou 3 navires qui accostent en même temps et qu’ils sont en même temps traités, c’est un plus pour nous», a dit le directeur général de la SOBEMAP. «Ils ont des engins mais qui ne marchent pas parce qu’ils ont des pièces qui sont gâtées», a renchéri Samuel Batcho.
L’entretien des machines
Le directeur général du Port autonome de Cotonou a expliqué au ministre que l’entretien des machines devant être assuré par des prestataires privés, est également soumis aux dispositions en matière de passation de marchés publics. Il a salué la visite du ministre qui, pour lui, vise la mobilisation des troupes. Il a porté à la connaissance du au ministre les difficultés qui sont criardes notamment au niveau de la SOBEMAP. « Quand l’engin d’un manutentionnaire privé tombe en panne, leurs pièces de rechange sont immédiatement commandées et il peut fonctionner à nouveau. Mais en ce qui concerne la SOBEMAP, il faut attendre six mois en raison des dispositions du code des marchés publics. Il faut toute une procédure pour l’achat des pièces des engins. Tout le gouvernement devrait se mobiliser afin de sauter certains verrous en ce qui concerne les activités portuaires», a laissé entendre le directeur général du Port autonome de Cotonou. 
«C’est avec satisfaction que je touche du doigt ce qui se fait ici. Ma visite sur les installations de la SOBEMAP notamment son dispositif de manutention, révèle quelques difficultés. Je note bien les doléances des directeurs généraux et d’ici à là, elles seront satisfaites. Des efforts seront faits par le gouvernement pour acheter des engins à la société afin de rendre plus compétitif notre Port. Le gouvernement est en train de mettre en œuvre un certain nombre de réformes afin de faciliter la tâche aux usagers de l’espace portuaire », a indiqué Patrick Yérima.
Le directeur général du PAC, Samuel Batcho a fait visiter au ministre de l’Economie maritime et des Infrastructures portuaires, les services clés du Port. Le Centre de contrôle et de surveillance, les quais nord et sud, le poste de contrôle et de délivrance des macarons, l’épi d’arrêt de sable construit avec le concours financier du Millennium challenge account (MCA) ainsi que le terminal Bolloré ont été visités par Patrick Yérima.
Par Sênoudé P. TOMETISSI & Bonaventure AGBON (stag)

The Minister in charge of the Maritime Economy, Patrick Yerima, made a visit yesterday, Tuesday 4 August, to the Autonomous Port of Cotonou (PAC) and to the installations of the Beninese Port Handling Company (SOBEMAP). The aim was to get first-hand knowledge of the problems facing the employees and users of these companies under the supervision of his ministerial department.

Patrick Yerima took the reins of the Ministry of the Maritime Economy and Port Infrastructure a few weeks ago, following the latest cabinet reshuffle. It was in order to gain a broader view of the activities carried out by the structures under his supervision that he toured the strategic services of the Autonomous Port of Cotonou and of the Beninese Port Handling Company (SOBEMAP) yesterday, Tuesday 4 August.

On arriving within the grounds of the Autonomous Port of Cotonou, Minister Patrick Yerima held a working session with the director general of the PAC, Samuel Batcho, and with that of SOBEMAP, Antoine Kouton, before visiting the port infrastructure.

The director general of SOBEMAP gave him a brief description of how the machinery used for loading and unloading containers operates. The equipment, of various brands, occupies dozens of metres on the company's premises. Antoine Kouton explained to the minister the difficulties his company faces. Sometimes the equipment's parts break down in the middle of an operation, and their spare parts require strict observance of the rules prescribed by the Public Procurement Code, which prohibits direct-award contracts. "If there are 2 or 3 ships berthing at the same time and they are handled at the same time, that is a plus for us," said the director general of SOBEMAP. "They have equipment but it does not work because they have parts that are damaged," added Samuel Batcho.

Machinery maintenance

The director general of the Autonomous Port of Cotonou explained to the minister that maintenance of the machinery, which is supposed to be provided by private contractors, is also subject to public procurement provisions. He welcomed the minister's visit, which in his view aims at rallying the troops. He brought to the minister's attention the glaring difficulties, particularly at SOBEMAP. "When a private handler's equipment breaks down, their spare parts are ordered immediately and it can operate again. But as far as SOBEMAP is concerned, you have to wait six months because of the provisions of the public procurement code. A whole procedure is required to buy the equipment's parts. The entire government should mobilise in order to remove certain locks as regards port activities," said the director general of the Autonomous Port of Cotonou.

"It is with satisfaction that I see first-hand what is being done here. My visit to SOBEMAP's installations, in particular its handling equipment, reveals some difficulties. I take good note of the directors general's requests, and between now and then they will be satisfied. Efforts will be made by the government to buy equipment for the company in order to make our Port more competitive. The government is implementing a number of reforms in order to make things easier for users of the port area," said Patrick Yerima.

The director general of the PAC, Samuel Batcho, took the Minister of the Maritime Economy and Port Infrastructure on a tour of the Port's key services. The Control and Surveillance Centre, the north and south quays, the checkpoint and badge-issuing office, the sand groyne built with the financial support of the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA) as well as the Bollore terminal were visited by Patrick Yerima.

By Senoude P. TOMETISSI & Bonaventure AGBON (intern)

a6779.t:
Faisant l’objet de débats, la diaspora bond s’impose, aujourd’hui, comme une alternative de financement du développement et un levier stratégique de transformation structurelle des économies en Afrique.
Un Forum libéral de promotion des diasporas bonds, initié par la Fondation Friedrich Naumann, s’est tenu ce jeudi 11 septembre 2025, à Abidjan, en présence d’économistes et des acteurs du secteur public.
Mme Alexandra Heldt, directrice régionale Afrique de l’Ouest de la Fondation Friedrich Naumann, a relevé que « l’Afrique possède en elle-même les forces nécessaires pour façonner son avenir. Et, dans ce processus, la diaspora joue un rôle stratégique ».
Chaque année, dira-t-elle, des milliards sont transférés vers le continent, témoignant de l’attachement profond des diasporas à leur terre d’origine. Toutefois, « le véritable défi est désormais de transformer cette solidarité financière en investissements productifs, capables de soutenir durablement l’innovation, les infrastructures, l’éducation, la santé et l’entrepreneuriat ».
« Les diaspora bonds (emprunts obligataires émis par les Etats) ne sont pas de simples instruments financiers, ils symbolisent un lien fort entre les citoyens et leurs nations, entre le passé et l’avenir, entre le désir d’appartenance et l’exigence de développement », a déclaré Mme Alexandra Heldt.
Ils incarnent, en outre, une approche libérale fondée sur la liberté, la responsabilité et l’engagement volontaire, permettant à chacun de contribuer au progrès de sa communauté, non par contrainte, mais par conviction, a-t-elle fait savoir.
« A la Fondation Friedrich Naumann, nous croyons fermement que la prospérité durable naît de la liberté économique, de la créativité et de la responsabilité citoyenne et les diaspora bonds illustrent cette vision : une solution africaine, portée par des Africains, pour construire un avenir commun », a-t-elle souligné.
La liberté économique est, aujourd’hui, plus que jamais d’actualité dans un monde où les conflits remplacent trop souvent le dialogue et la coopération. Pour elle, les pays africains devraient gagner en indépendance vis-à-vis des financements étrangers.
« Les guerres en Europe et au Moyen-Orient, tout comme le recul de l’aide américaine, nous obligent à repenser et optimiser nos ressources, investir de manière responsable et durable », a fait observer la directrice régionale Afrique de l’Ouest de la Fondation Friedrich Naumann.
Lanciné Diaby, le directeur général des financements au ministère ivoirien des Finances et du Budget, a noté que les transferts de fonds émanant de la diaspora africaine sont des ressources précieuses pour leurs pays d’origine.
D’ailleurs, la communauté des émigrés africains compterait aujourd’hui pas moins de 140 millions d’individus à travers le monde, selon la Banque mondiale. Par conséquent, la diaspora africaine constitue une véritable puissance économique.
En 2024, les transferts de fonds vers l’Afrique ont atteint 92,2 milliards de dollars, soit environ 5,2% du PIB du continent et devraient dépasser les 100 milliards de dollars en 2025, a rappelé le directeur général des financements.
Ces transferts de fonds représentent une source de financements extérieurs aussi importante que l’aide publique au développement et les investissements directs étrangers. De surcroît, ils participent de manière significative à la stabilité macroéconomique en renforçant les réserves en devises étrangères.
Les cas d’école ne manquent pas. Depuis les expériences pionnières d’Israël et de l’Inde au milieu du XXème siècle, de nombreux pays africains tels que l’Ethiopie, le Nigéria et le Sénégal ont émis avec succès des diaspora bonds, a indiqué Prof Séraphin Prao, un éminent économiste ivoirien.
Prof Séraphin Prao a fait remarquer qu’il faut que l’Etat inspire confiance pour pouvoir attirer les devises étrangères à travers la diaspora bond, avoir une vision à long terme assortie à des projets innovants et surtout faire des placements stratégiques.
Pour sa part, M. Stanislas Zézé, patron d’une agence de notation financière, a invité les dirigeants à repenser le modèle de financement des économies africaines, mentionnant qu’avec 54 pays dont les monnaies sont inconvertibles, ce mécanisme ne sera pas exploité à fond.
Il a appelé à régler la convertibilité des monnaies et surtout à briser les barrières d’emprunts inter-Etats, tout en évoquant l’ouverture de la diaspora bond à d’autres pays étrangers selon les thématiques qui gouvernent à la mobilisation des ressources.
Aujourd’hui, avec un volume total émis estimé à plus de 50 milliards de dollars à l’échelle mondiale, ces instruments représentent une classe d’actifs d’avenir. Depuis plusieurs années, la Côte d’Ivoire, dans sa stratégie de financement, fait du développement du marché local une priorité.
AP/Sf/APA
a6779.en:
RCI: debate over the stakes and limits of the diaspora bond

The subject of debate, the diaspora bond is today establishing itself as an alternative means of financing development and a strategic lever for the structural transformation of Africa's economies.

A Liberal Forum for the promotion of diaspora bonds, initiated by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, was held on Thursday 11 September 2025 in Abidjan, in the presence of economists and public-sector actors.

Ms Alexandra Heldt, West Africa Regional Director of the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, noted that "Africa possesses within itself the forces necessary to shape its own future. And in this process, the diaspora plays a strategic role."

Every year, she said, billions are transferred to the continent, testifying to the diasporas' deep attachment to their land of origin. However, "the real challenge is now to transform this financial solidarity into productive investments capable of sustainably supporting innovation, infrastructure, education, health and entrepreneurship."

"Diaspora bonds (bond issues floated by states) are not mere financial instruments; they symbolise a strong link between citizens and their nations, between the past and the future, between the desire to belong and the demand for development," declared Ms Alexandra Heldt.

They also embody, she indicated, a liberal approach founded on freedom, responsibility and voluntary commitment, allowing each person to contribute to the progress of their community, not out of constraint, but out of conviction.

"At the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, we firmly believe that lasting prosperity is born of economic freedom, creativity and civic responsibility, and diaspora bonds illustrate this vision: an African solution, carried by Africans, to build a common future," she underlined.

Economic freedom is today more topical than ever in a world where conflict too often replaces dialogue and cooperation. For her, African countries should gain independence from foreign financing.

"The wars in Europe and the Middle East, just like the retreat of American aid, oblige us to rethink and optimise our resources, and to invest responsibly and sustainably," observed the West Africa Regional Director of the Friedrich Naumann Foundation.

Lanciné Diaby, Director General of Financing at the Ivorian Ministry of Finance and Budget, noted that remittances from the African diaspora are precious resources for their countries of origin.

Indeed, the community of African emigrants today reportedly numbers no fewer than 140 million individuals worldwide, according to the World Bank. Consequently, the African diaspora constitutes a genuine economic power.

In 2024, remittances to Africa reached $92.2 billion, about 5.2% of the continent's GDP, and should exceed $100 billion in 2025, recalled the Director General of Financing.

These remittances represent a source of external financing as important as official development assistance and foreign direct investment. Moreover, they contribute significantly to macroeconomic stability by strengthening foreign currency reserves.

There is no shortage of textbook cases. Since the pioneering experiences of Israel and India in the middle of the 20th century, many African countries such as Ethiopia, Nigeria and Senegal have successfully issued diaspora bonds, indicated Prof Séraphin Prao, an eminent Ivorian economist.

Prof Séraphin Prao remarked that the state must inspire confidence in order to be able to attract foreign currency through the diaspora bond, must have a long-term vision matched with innovative projects, and above all must make strategic investments.

For his part, Mr Stanislas Zézé, head of a financial rating agency, invited leaders to rethink the model for financing African economies, mentioning that with 54 countries whose currencies are non-convertible, this mechanism will not be fully exploited.

He called for the question of currency convertibility to be settled and above all for the barriers to inter-state borrowing to be broken, while raising the possibility of opening the diaspora bond to other foreign countries according to the themes governing resource mobilisation.

Today, with a total volume issued estimated at more than $50 billion worldwide, these instruments represent an asset class of the future. For several years, Côte d'Ivoire, in its financing strategy, has made the development of the local market a priority.

AP/Sf/APA

….Warns GBA against acting as ‘Wing of Opposition Party’
The Majority Chief Whip, Rockson-Nelson Dafeamekpor, has accused the Ghana Bar Association (GBA) of politically sidelining President John Dramani Mahama in its upcoming annual conference, questioning the association’s impartiality and commitment to fairness.
In a strongly worded statement, Mr Dafeamekpor, a lawyer by profession and a member of the GBA, criticized that while former President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo was almost always featured as a Special Guest of Honour and keynote speaker at GBA conferences between 2017 and 2024, the current President’s name was conspicuously missing from the 2025 programme.
“I have observed how the GBA organised its annual conference from 2017 to 2024. The then President, Nana Akufo-Addo, was nearly always the Special Guest of Honour and Speaker. That is not the case in 2025. The President is conspicuously missing from the list of advertised speakers at the confab,” he stated on the social media platform X.
Efua Ghartey, the current President of the GBA. She is the wife ofJoe Ghartey, formerly the Member of Parliament (MP) for Essikado-Ketan on the ticket of the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP).
Mr Dafeamekpor expressed particular concern that, instead of inviting President Mahama, the GBA leadership had extended an invitation to the President of the Bar Council of England and Wales, a body which he said recently attacked the Ghanaian government “without provocation,” reference the group’s statement in condemning the suspension of Chief Justice Gertrude Araba Asaaba Sackey Torkornoo.
“The GBA leadership has rather decided to invite the President of the Bar Council of England and Wales. GBA, kindly add the President of the Commonwealth Lawyers Association for effect,” he said in a sarcastic remark.
The Majority Chief Whip accused the GBA of displaying “unalloyed bias” against President Mahama and the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC), suggesting that the association was acting in the interest of the main opposition party.
“Your bias against John Mahama and the NDC government is too glaring to be ignored now. You can continue to act as a wing of the main opposition party to do its bidding we are ready for you,” he declared.
“What is curious,” he wrote in a social media post, “is that the GBA leadership has instead chosen to invite the President of the Bar Council of England and Wales, a group that recently attacked this government without any provocation.”
The Majority Chief Whip suggested that the association should also consider inviting the President of the Commonwealth Lawyers Association “for effect.” He accused the GBA of showing “unalloyed bias” against President Mahama and the governing National Democratic Congress.
“You can continue to act as a wing of the main opposition party to do its bidding,” Dafeamekpor added. “We are ready for you.”
The GBA has not yet responded to the allegations.
However, this is not the first time that Mr Dafeamekpor, has berated the GBA. Following reports that the association passed a resolution calling on President Mahama to revoke the suspension of Chief Justice Torkornoo, the MP went to town on the Association.
In a post shared on social media on Sunday, April 27, 2025, Dafeamekpor, a lawyer himself, stated that the resolution, if indeed true, constitutes contempt of the Supreme Court’s power.
He pointed out that the action of the GBA also amounts to an interference with the functions of the judiciary and a violation of the code of conduct for lawyers in Ghana.
“Our very own Code of Conduct, the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct & Etiquette) Rules, 2020, LI 2423, forbids any lawyer or leaders of any lawyers’ grouping from running any such unguarded commentaries or making such unprofessional public demands on a live case. Indeed, Regulation 89(c) of LI 2423, 2020 states as follows: ‘a lawyer commits professional misconduct where the lawyer engages in a conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice’.
“The above provision forbids any member of the Bar or its leaders from upending the rights of one party in a case against the other part (ies). What the GBA leadership is engaged in is a front to the administration of justice and has the propensity to torpedo the independence of the judiciary they ostensibly seek to protect, the Majority Chief Whip of Parliament wrote.
He asserted that the resolution was politically motivated, urging President Mahama to ignore it if it is indeed brought before him.
“This reported call by the GBA is very partisan & prejudicial as it affects a matter sub judice.
“The GBA leadership, like Caesar’s wife, must live above reproach. I urge His Excellency, the President, to ignore this illicit public call by the GBA leadership as if same was never made, for it is a wrong call. It is better for a law to be wrong than for a wrong to be law,” his post concluded.
The GBA has reportedly passed a resolution to call on President Mahama to revoke the suspension of Chief Justice Torkornoo.
According to a report by thelawplatform. online, the resolution was passed at the GBA’s Mid-Year Conference held at Labadi Beach Hotel in Accra on April 26, 2025.
The report indicated that members of the Bar were displeased with the suspension of the Chief Justice after getting details of the three petitions for her removal.
They were also not happy with the determination of a prima facie case in the three petitions filed for Justice Torkornoo’s removal by President Mahama and the Council of State.
The members of the GBA also expressed their displeasure with the association’s leadership over a statement issued regarding the ongoing process for removing the Chief Justice.
They indicated that they were not happy with the import and tone of the statement, which was dated April 24, 2025.
The GBA also indicated that it would present a petition challenging the removal of the Chief Justice.

Que balanço é que faz desta 4ª Cimeira dos SIDS? Que conclusões é que é possível tirar deste encontro?
Bom, nós estamos a falar de um balanço muito positivo, um trabalho longo que decorreu ao longo de vários meses, incluindo com discussões que tiveram lugar em Cabo Verde, e, portanto, quando chegamos aqui a esta reunião internacional, o trabalho no essencial estava feito e, portanto, estamos a falar de uma grande convergência, ao contrário do que muitas vezes acontece em cimeiras internacionais em que as negociações se arrastam. Neste caso, estamos a falar de uma grande convergência do ponto de vista quanto ao essencial que é mobilizar todos os esforços para apoiar os pequenos estados insulares que enfrentam níveis de vulnerabilidade sem precedentes. Hoje, ninguém tem dúvidas que os pequenos estados insulares estão numa situação muito difícil. São aqueles que mais consequências enfrentam das alterações climáticas. Em termos prácticos, estes 39 países representam dois terços dos países mais afectados pelas consequências da mudança climática. São países que enfrentam as consequências de choques económicos globais, que enfrentam os problemas relacionados com o tamanho, com a distância, a dificuldade de conectividade e depois também os níveis de dívida muito significativos. Neste momento, cerca de 40% dos pequenos Estados insulares estão com níveis de dívida insustentáveis ou próximos disso. Portanto, a primeira grande conclusão de que eu gostaria de tirar desta Cimeira é que houve uma total convergência de pontos de vista quanto à necessidade da comunidade internacional apoiar os pequenos Estados insulares para enfrentar a vulnerabilidade. E houve também uma grande convergência quanto à forma de o fazer. Isso passa pela concretização do Plano de Acção de 10 anos, este plano que se chama ABAS (Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS). Este plano, de uma forma muito detalhada, enumera um conjunto de acções, de projectos, de reformas que são necessárias. E também, como é evidente, faz uma forte convocatória para a mobilização de recursos financeiros adicionais. E, desse ponto de vista, se me permite, há aqui uma área onde penso que se alcança um progresso muito importante, que há muitos, muitos anos os pequenos Estados Insulares reclamavam, que era olhar para a vulnerabilidade com uma métrica que não passa apenas pelo PIB per capita, o rendimento nacional bruto per capita. E existe hoje um conceito muito alargado quanto à introdução de uma métrica que é o Multidimensional Vulnerability Index, portanto, o índice de vulnerabilidade multidimensional que permite aferir as vulnerabilidades, as fragilidades, as dificuldades que os SIDS enfrentam, além do PIB per capita. Ora, esta métrica não vai substituir o PIB per capita, não vai criar uma dicotomia entre uma métrica e outra. Na prática, traz mais informação e colecta informação adicional. Aquilo que se espera é que exista financiamento adicional, seja financiamento concessional, portanto ajuda pública ao desenvolvimento, seja financiamento privado. Portanto, no fundo, nós saímos aqui de Antígua e Barbuda com uma clara missão para concretizar projectos essenciais na área da economia azul, da economia verde, da descarbonização, da adaptação às alterações climáticas, da diversificação da economia nos pequenos estados insulares, para não ficarem tão dependentes, por exemplo, do turismo, uma maior conectividade dos pequenos Estados insulares com outros países, o reforço do comércio, o reforço das infraestruturas essenciais na água, no saneamento, na energia, nas telecomunicações. Há aqui uma mobilização muito grande em relação à acção. Finalmente, há um dado adicional que me parece importante, é que desta vez este plano vai ter um mecanismo de avaliação e monitorização. Este é o quarto plano de acção. Já tivemos três planos de acção e uma das grandes diferenças é que desta vez este plano vai ter mecanismos de avaliação e de reporte. E este plano não é um plano dos SIDS, é um plano para os SIDS. O que é que isso significa? Que não são os pequenos Estados insulares que vão ser avaliados na concretização deste plano, é toda a comunidade internacional, incluindo os doadores. E isso é o que vai impedir aqui um nível de accountability muito importante. Eu gostava de acrescentar uma coisa que tem a ver com financiamento inovador e com o tema da dívida. E parece-me importante sublinhar que o exemplo de Cabo Verde foi referido em múltiplas questões, já tinha verificado isso em conferências anteriores nos últimos meses, como um país que encontrou uma solução interessante, inovadora, para troca de dívida por investimento na área verde, na área azul, na área digital. E este mecanismo que em inglês se chama debt for climate e debt for nature, é um dos mecanismos que vai sendo referido como mecanismo inovador.
O primeiro-ministro de Cabo Verde, que esteve presente na Cimeira, falou sobre a questão das dificuldades de financiamento dos SIDS. Como é que isto se pode modificar de forma a que seja mais fácil o acesso ao financiamento por parte destes países?
Há três áreas onde isso é decisivo. Do lado da oferta, do lado da procura e do lado da própria organização do mercado. Do lado da oferta, precisamos mobilizar mais financiamento para os SIDS, mais financiamento público, nomeadamente a ajuda pública ao desenvolvimento, mas também mecanismos inovadores como o financiamento misto, que é o blended finance, em que se combina financiamento público e financiamento privado, o investimento de impacto, o esvaziamento das linhas de crédito externas. Também reformas fiscais, nomeadamente a nível internacional, eliminando os subsídios aos combustíveis fósseis para mobilizar mais recursos financeiros para as áreas de acção climática, o desenvolvimento dos mercados de carbono. Portanto, estas áreas são áreas fundamentais para mobilizar os recursos que são necessários. E estamos a falar de níveis de grandeza muito significativos. Só para lhe dar uma ideia: os SIDS precisarão, nos próximos 10 anos, de 70 mil milhões de dólares para financiamento a infraestruturas. Neste momento, os SIDS recebem de ajuda pública ao desenvolvimento cerca de 3 ou 4 mil milhões de dólares. Portanto, repare a diferença entre as duas ordens de grandeza. O financiamento público internacional não vai ser suficiente. Vai ser preciso aumentar este financiamento, mais financiamento público, mais ajuda pública ao desenvolvimento, mas também mobilizar investimento privado, como eu referi com os outros mecanismos que enunciei. Em segundo lugar, é preciso o lado da procura também criar condições para atrair investimento. Isso significa que os pequenos estados insulares terão de desenvolver reforma políticas, reformas estruturais para criar um ambiente regulatório que atraia o investimento. Vou-lhe dar um exemplo: nunca haverá condições para se fazer investimento público e privado em adaptação às alterações climáticas se os países não tiverem políticas de ordenamento do território compatíveis com a redução dos riscos climáticos, ou políticas de gestão dos recursos hídricos que reduzam a sua utilização intensiva. Não haverá investimento público ou privado nas energias renováveis se os países não tiverem feito reformas no ambiente regulatório na remuneração das energias renováveis. Portanto, esta segunda dimensão é uma dimensão também muito importante. As reformas políticas, o ambiente de contexto para atrair investimento. E há uma terceira área que me parece também muito importante, que tem a ver com a capacidade. Muitas vezes temos o dinheiro, temos as políticas implementadas, as reformas, mas falta capacidade técnica. Ora, é fundamental também que a comunidade internacional se mobilize para parcerias de cooperação para reforço das competências nas áreas de desenho de projectos, da concretização de projectos. Isto do lado da oferta e do lado da procura. Depois há uma terceira dimensão que tem a ver com a própria organização do mercado. Quando eu digo mercado, é do mercado de financiamento ao desenvolvimento, que é o acesso aos próprios mecanismos de acesso aos bancos multilaterais e às instituições financeiras. Ora, o secretário-geral das Nações Unidas tem vindo a defender uma reforma do sistema financeiro internacional para que os SIDS tenham mais representação, mais voz, mais participação, mais direito de voto, para que possa haver mais liquidez atribuída aos SIDS para que exista mais capacidade de concessão de crédito destas agências. Portanto, no fundo, nós precisamos de reformas nas três dimensões. Mais financiamento internacional, mais reformas políticas nos SIDS para atrair este investimento e uma reforma da arquitectura financeira internacional.
Cabo Verde tem vindo a apostar na economia verde, na economia azul, e está a apostar também a digitalização. Este é um caminho certo?
Sem dúvida. Essa é a agenda certa. A agenda do crescimento azul e do crescimento verde, no fundo, a agenda da descarbonização, não só para reduzir as emissões, mas para criar emprego, para criar empresas na área das tecnologias limpas, das energias renováveis e da eficiência energética, é a agenda certa. A agenda de proteger os oceanos, mas ao mesmo tempo de valorizar os oceanos do ponto de vista económico, não só com os sectores tradicionais, como as pescas, mas também com novas actividades como a energia offshore, a biotecnologia, é a agenda certa. Depois há também uma agenda incontornável, que é a agenda digital. Hoje, em especial para os SIDS, que estão tão desligados territorialmente de outros países, o digital é essencial. É essencial para a igualdade de oportunidades, para que as crianças possam ter acesso ao nível de educação que merecem, para que a sociedade se organize de uma forma mais transparente e menos burocrática, mas também para que o comércio se faça, porque hoje o comércio digital tem um peso muito grande. Portanto, eu não tenho dúvidas nenhumas que a agenda verde, a agenda azul e a agenda digital são as agendas não só amigas do ambiente e amigas da dimensão social do desenvolvimento, mas também amigas do crescimento, da competitividade e da criação de emprego.
Como melhorar a atractividade dos SIDS, e especificamente de Cabo Verde, para que seja capaz de convencer quem está lá fora de que Cabo Verde é um país em que vale a pena apostar?
Esse é o ponto importante. É necessário que a comunidade internacional se mobilize para apoiar os países. A comunidade internacional fala do sector público e do sector privado, para apoiar os pequenos estados insulares, porque são mais vulneráveis, mas também mobilizar para que apoiem, porque é um bom investimento. Não se trata apenas de solidariedade, e a solidariedade é essencial. Trata-se também de mobilizar investimento, porque é um investimento reprodutivo, e, portanto, eu acho que esta lógica de valorizar actividades económicas mais diversificadas, não pôr, como sói-se dizer, os ovos todos no mesmo cesto, no cesto do turismo, ou no cesto das pescas, ou no cesto da agricultura. No fundo, ter uma actividade económica diversificada. E além de ser diversificada, muito centrada nos sectores onde o crescimento é mais acelerado, que é, como estamos a falar, a economia verde, nomeadamente, isso parece-me uma margem importante. Eu costumo sempre dizer, até quando falava do meu país, eu, como sabe, tive funções governamentais em Portugal, eu costumava sempre dizer que existem 460 triliões de dólares, portanto 460 biliões de dólares, disponíveis nos mercados financeiros, nos fundos de pensões e no mercado de capitais. E no fundo os países têm de fazer tudo o que podem, no plano das políticas nacionais, mas também no plano da diplomacia internacional, para que esse financiamento possa ser atraível. Porque há uma competição global. E, portanto, eu acho que nesta equação de grandes vulnerabilidades que têm os SIDS, mas também de um fundo financeiro que está disponível à escala global, que é também muito significativo, é importante que a comunidade internacional se mobilize para apoiar mais os pequenos estados internacionais, mas também que os pequenos estados internacionais possam realizar as suas políticas para atrair mais investimento. Eu acho que estas duas dimensões são importantes do lado da oferta, para que haja mais solidariedade e mais mobilização com aqueles que são mais vulneráveis, mas também do lado da procura, para que a atracção de investimento seja mais alinhada com estas altas agendas das alterações climáticas e totalmente sustentável.
Cabo Verde tem problema de escala. O caminho é, então, a internacionalização do sector privado?
Eu preferia não me pronunciar sobre as agendas nacionais, porque há uma boa regra, que é, obviamente, que as políticas nacionais competem aos países, aos governos democraticamente eleitos. Portanto, eu não quero estar a receber uma avaliação das políticas nacionais, até porque, sinceramente, não tenho conhecimento suficiente sobre o dia-a-dia da política nacional, posso dizer, em qualquer caso, daquilo que vou observando nas reuniões internacionais, com a participação do Primeiro-Ministro, do Ministro dos Negócios Estrangeiros, o que me parece evidente é que Cabo Verde se está a fazer muito nestas discussões internacionais, pelo facto de não estar só a reclamar mais solidariedade internacional, mas estar também a demonstrar uma vontade de liderar temas tão importantes como a Agenda Digital, a Agenda Verde e a Agenda Azul.
Mas falando genericamente dos SIDS, a escala é uma dificuldade que existe. Estamos a falar de países que têm o mesmo número de habitantes que uma cidade média europeia. Como é que esses países tendo em conta que têm pouca mão de obra, poderão ser estimulantes para o investimento inteiro?
Eu julgo que a questão da escala não é ultrapassável, portanto, é a realidade com que têm de viver, mas a dimensão da conectividade é ultrapassável. E, portanto, uma das dimensões importantes é o reforço da conectividade, dos pequenos estados insulares com outros países. E a conectividade tem a ver com os transportes, com a componente digital e com o comércio. Portanto, isto parece-me essencial. Mas há sempre uma dimensão inultrapassável, como disse bem, que é, além da distância e do problema da conectividade, que é a própria escala. A escala torna este investimento mais oneroso. E por isso é preciso que a comunidade internacional não perca isso de vista. Nós sabemos, por exemplo, que na ajuda pública ao desenvolvimento, aquilo que os doadores atribuem ao desenvolvimento, quando se trata de projectos em pequenos estados insulares, o custo é quatro vezes maior. É quatro vezes maior porque a escala é menor, o custo para usar os materiais é maior, as vulnerabilidades, nomeadamente climáticas, são maiores, com consequências na elaboração e na concretização de projectos, e depois as infraestruturas são mais caras porque é preciso que sejam mais resilientes para enfrentar a falta de água, os choques climáticos extremos. Portanto, por isso é que eu tenho referido que, além do trabalho que os governos fazem, que os países fazem e os pequenos estados insulares fazem, a comunidade internacional tem a obrigação moral de se mobilizar para apoiar estes países, porque há níveis de vulnerabilidade que são quase inultrapassáveis. Tem a ver com a realidade geográfica, com a realidade climática e com a própria natureza destes territórios. Portanto, é obrigatório uma mobilização internacional. Mas qual é a dificuldade que estes países enfrentam do ponto de vista do acesso ao financiamento internacional? É que muitos deles têm níveis de PIB per capita que deixou de os tornar elegíveis para ajuda pública ao desenvolvimento, porque tornaram-se países de rendimento alto, ou até, como foi o caso de Cabo Verde, graduou-se de país menos desenvolvido para país de rendimento médio. O que é que significa? Apesar de ser ainda elegível para ajuda ao desenvolvimento, deixou de ser prioritário. Ora, estes países que, estatisticamente, têm um PIB per capita mais elevado, podem perder tudo com um desastre natural, como aconteceu, quer nas Caraíbas, quer no Pacífico, com muita frequência. Portanto, não se pode olhar apenas para a dimensão estatística do PIB, é importante olhar para a vulnerabilidade. E, por isso, é que este indicador que eu me referi de vulnerabilidade multidirecional é tão importante, porque vai permitir que, quem está numa agência de desenvolvimento, num país doador, quem está num banco de desenvolvimento, quem está num banco de investimento, quando tem de tomar decisões de financiamento aos países, não olhe apenas para o PIB per capita, mas olhe também para a vulnerabilidade desses países. Portanto, o tema da solidariedade internacional é crucial. E eu julgo, sinceramente, que esta cimeira conseguiu alcançar níveis históricos de convergência com a agenda dos SIDS. Agora é preciso passar à acção. E as agências das Nações Unidas, como o UNOPS e as outras agências, obviamente, têm que estar disponíveis para as parcerias no terreno, para contribuir para a concretização de projectos, nomeadamente, das infraestruturas.
Ulisses Correia e Silva, na participação que fez na Cimeira, defendeu que os SIDS têm de escapar à armadilha do PIB per capita. Concorda com essa ideia? O PIB per capita é uma armadilha, realmente?
Eu não sei se é uma armadilha. Tem sido uma métrica que não tem sido suficientemente robusta para lidar com os pequenos estados de esforço. Portanto, no fundo, nós temos métricas que, obviamente, têm que corresponder à realidade e o PIB per capita, que vai ter de continuar a ser utilizado para muitas decisões, não pode ser a única métrica. Por isso, este indicador de vulnerabilidade multidimensional é um bom contributo.
Uma última questão. No actual cenário político a nível internacional, com o surgimento de partidos e governos extremistas e, por isso, menos interessados na cooperação internacional, é possível concretizar esta agenda dos SIDS?
Num mundo cada vez mais interdependente, todos ficamos a ganhar com acréscimo de solidariedade com os mais vulneráveis. A solução para os grandes problemas globais passa por mais multilateralismo e mais cooperação e não por fechamento ou intolerância.
Texto originalmente publicado na edição impressa do Expresso das Ilhas nº 1175 de 5 de Junho de 2024.

What is your assessment of this 4th SIDS Summit? What conclusions can be drawn from this meeting?

Well, we are talking about a very positive assessment, a long piece of work that unfolded over several months, including discussions that took place in Cabo Verde, and so, when we arrived here at this international meeting, the work was essentially done, and therefore we are talking about a great convergence, contrary to what often happens at international summits where the negotiations drag on. In this case, we are talking about a great convergence of views as to the essential point, which is to mobilise all efforts to support the small island states that are facing unprecedented levels of vulnerability. Today, no one has any doubt that the small island states are in a very difficult situation. They are the ones that face the most consequences of climate change. In practical terms, these 39 countries represent two thirds of the countries most affected by the consequences of climate change. They are countries that face the consequences of global economic shocks, that face the problems related to size, to distance, to the difficulty of connectivity, and then also very significant levels of debt. At this moment, about 40% of small island States have unsustainable levels of debt or close to that. Therefore, the first major conclusion that I would like to draw from this Summit is that there was a total convergence of points of view as to the need for the international community to support the small island States in facing vulnerability. And there was also a great convergence as to the way of doing it. That goes through the implementation of the 10-year Action Plan, this plan that is called ABAS (Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS). This plan, in a very detailed way, lists a set of actions, of projects, of reforms that are necessary. And it also, obviously, makes a strong call for the mobilisation of additional financial resources. And, from that point of view, if you will allow me, there is an area here where I think very important progress is achieved, something that for many, many years the small island States had been demanding, which was to look at vulnerability with a metric that does not go only through GDP per capita, gross national income per capita. And there exists today a very broad concept as to the introduction of a metric which is the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index, therefore the multidimensional vulnerability index, which makes it possible to gauge the vulnerabilities, the fragilities, the difficulties that the SIDS face, beyond GDP per capita. Now, this metric is not going to replace GDP per capita, it is not going to create a dichotomy between one metric and another. In practice, it brings more information and collects additional information. What is expected is that there should be additional financing, whether concessional financing, that is, official development assistance, or private financing. So, in essence, we leave here from Antigua and Barbuda with a clear mission to deliver essential projects in the area of the blue economy, the green economy, decarbonisation, adaptation to climate change, diversification of the economy in the small island states, so that they do not remain so dependent, for example, on tourism, greater connectivity of the small island States with other countries, the strengthening of trade, the strengthening of essential infrastructure in water, sanitation, energy and telecommunications. There is a very great mobilisation here with regard to action. Finally, there is one additional element that seems important to me, which is that this time this plan will have an evaluation and monitoring mechanism. This is the fourth action plan. We have already had three action plans and one of the great differences is that this time this plan will have evaluation and reporting mechanisms. And this plan is not a plan of the SIDS, it is a plan for the SIDS. What does that mean? That it is not the small island States that are going to be evaluated on the implementation of this plan, it is the whole international community, including the donors. And that is what will ensure a very important level of accountability here. I would like to add something that has to do with innovative financing and with the debt issue. And it seems important to me to underline that the example of Cabo Verde was referred to in multiple matters - I had already noted this at previous conferences in recent months - as a country that found an interesting, innovative solution for exchanging debt for investment in the green area, the blue area and the digital area. And this mechanism, which in English is called debt for climate and debt for nature, is one of the mechanisms that is being referred to as an innovative mechanism.

The Prime Minister of Cabo Verde, who was present at the Summit, spoke about the question of the SIDS' financing difficulties. How can this be changed so that access to financing by these countries becomes easier?

There are three areas where this is decisive. On the supply side, on the demand side and on the side of the organisation of the market itself. On the supply side, we need to mobilise more financing for the SIDS, more public financing, namely official development assistance, but also innovative mechanisms such as mixed financing, which is blended finance, in which public financing and private financing are combined, impact investment, the drawing down of external credit lines. Also fiscal reforms, namely at international level, eliminating subsidies for fossil fuels in order to mobilise more financial resources for the areas of climate action, the development of carbon markets. So, these areas are fundamental areas for mobilising the resources that are needed. And we are talking about very significant orders of magnitude. Just to give you an idea: the SIDS will need, over the next 10 years, 70 billion dollars for infrastructure financing. At this moment, the SIDS receive about 3 or 4 billion dollars in official development assistance. So, note the difference between the two orders of magnitude. International public financing is not going to be enough. It will be necessary to increase this financing - more public financing, more official development assistance - but also to mobilise private investment, as I mentioned with the other mechanisms that I set out. Secondly, on the demand side it is also necessary to create conditions to attract investment. That means that the small island states will have to develop policy reforms, structural reforms, to create a regulatory environment that attracts investment. I will give you an example: there will never be conditions for public and private investment in adaptation to climate change if countries do not have spatial planning policies compatible with the reduction of climate risks, or water resource management policies that reduce their intensive use. There will be no public or private investment in renewable energies if countries have not carried out reforms in the regulatory environment for the remuneration of renewable energies. So, this second dimension is also a very important dimension. Policy reforms, the contextual environment for attracting investment. And there is a third area that also seems very important to me, which has to do with capacity. Often we have the money, we have the policies implemented, the reforms, but technical capacity is lacking. Now, it is also fundamental that the international community mobilises for cooperation partnerships to strengthen skills in the areas of project design and project delivery. That is on the supply side and on the demand side. Then there is a third dimension that has to do with the organisation of the market itself. When I say market, it is the market of development financing, which is access to the very mechanisms of access to the multilateral banks and to the financial institutions. Now, the Secretary-General of the United Nations has been advocating a reform of the international financial system so that the SIDS have more representation, more voice, more participation, more voting rights, so that more liquidity can be allocated to the SIDS and so that there is more lending capacity on the part of these agencies. So, in essence, we need reforms in the three dimensions. More international financing, more policy reforms in the SIDS to attract this investment, and a reform of the international financial architecture.

Cabo Verde has been betting on the green economy, on the blue economy, and is also betting on digitalisation. Is this the right path?

Without a doubt. That is the right agenda. The agenda of blue growth and green growth, in essence the agenda of decarbonisation, not only to reduce emissions, but to create employment, to create companies in the area of clean technologies, of renewable energies and of energy efficiency, is the right agenda. The agenda of protecting the oceans, but at the same time of valuing the oceans from an economic point of view, not only with the traditional sectors, such as fisheries, but also with new activities such as offshore energy and biotechnology, is the right agenda. Then there is also an unavoidable agenda, which is the digital agenda. Today, especially for the SIDS, which are so territorially disconnected from other countries, the digital is essential. It is essential for equality of opportunity, so that children can have access to the level of education they deserve, so that society is organised in a more transparent and less bureaucratic way, but also so that trade can take place, because today digital commerce carries a very great weight. So, I have no doubt whatsoever that the green agenda, the blue agenda and the digital agenda are agendas that are not only friendly to the environment and friendly to the social dimension of development, but also friendly to growth, to competitiveness and to job creation.

How can the attractiveness of the SIDS, and specifically of Cabo Verde, be improved so that it is able to convince those abroad that Cabo Verde is a country worth betting on?

That is the important point. It is necessary for the international community to mobilise to support the countries. The international community means the public sector and the private sector, to support the small island states, because they are more vulnerable, but also to mobilise them to give support because it is a good investment. It is not only a matter of solidarity, and solidarity is essential. It is also a matter of mobilising investment, because it is a productive investment, and therefore I think that this logic of valuing more diversified economic activities, of not putting, as the saying goes, all the eggs in the same basket, in the basket of tourism, or in the basket of fisheries, or in the basket of agriculture. In essence, having a diversified economic activity. And besides being diversified, very much centred on the sectors where growth is fastest, which is, as we are saying, the green economy in particular - that seems to me an important margin. I always tend to say, even when I spoke of my own country - I, as you know, held governmental positions in Portugal - I always used to say that there are 460 trillion dollars available in the financial markets, in pension funds and in the capital market. And in essence countries have to do everything they can, at the level of national policies, but also at the level of international diplomacy, so that this financing can be attracted. Because there is global competition. And therefore I think that in this equation of great vulnerabilities that the SIDS have, but also of a financial pool that is available on a global scale, which is also very significant, it is important that the international community mobilises to support the small island states more, but also that the small island states are able to carry out their policies to attract more investment. I think these two dimensions are important, on the supply side, so that there is more solidarity and more mobilisation with those who are most vulnerable, but also on the demand side, so that the attraction of investment is more aligned with these high agendas of climate change and fully sustainable.

Cabo Verde has a problem of scale. Is the path, then, the internationalisation of the private sector?

I would prefer not to comment on national agendas, because there is a good rule, which is, obviously, that national policies are the responsibility of the countries, of democratically elected governments. So, I do not want to be making an assessment of national policies, all the more so because, sincerely, I do not have sufficient knowledge about the day-to-day of national politics. I can say, in any case, from what I observe at international meetings, with the participation of the Prime Minister, of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, what seems evident to me is that Cabo Verde is making itself felt a great deal in these international discussions, by the fact that it is not only demanding more international solidarity, but is also demonstrating a will to lead themes as important as the Digital Agenda, the Green Agenda and the Blue Agenda.

But speaking generally of the SIDS, scale is a difficulty that exists. We are talking about countries that have the same number of inhabitants as a medium-sized European city. How can these countries, bearing in mind that they have little labour force, be stimulating for investment as a whole?

I believe that the question of scale is not surmountable, so it is the reality they have to live with, but the dimension of connectivity is surmountable. And therefore one of the important dimensions is the strengthening of the connectivity of the small island states with other countries. And connectivity has to do with transport, with the digital component and with trade. So this seems essential to me. But there is always an insurmountable dimension, as you rightly said, which is, besides distance and the problem of connectivity, scale itself. Scale makes this investment more costly. And that is why the international community must not lose sight of this. We know, for example, that in official development assistance, in what donors allocate to development, when it is a matter of projects in small island states, the cost is four times higher. It is four times higher because the scale is smaller, the cost of using materials is higher, the vulnerabilities, namely climate vulnerabilities, are greater, with consequences for the design and delivery of projects, and then the infrastructure is more expensive because it needs to be more resilient in order to face water shortages and extreme climate shocks. So that is why I have said that, besides the work that governments do, that countries do and that the small island states do, the international community has the moral obligation to mobilise to support these countries, because there are levels of vulnerability that are almost insurmountable. It has to do with geographical reality, with climate reality and with the very nature of these territories. So an international mobilisation is obligatory. But what is the difficulty that these countries face from the point of view of access to international financing? It is that many of them have levels of GDP per capita that have made them no longer eligible for official development assistance, because they have become high-income countries, or even, as was the case with Cabo Verde, graduated from least developed country to middle-income country. What does that mean? Although it is still eligible for development aid, it has ceased to be a priority. Now, these countries which, statistically, have a higher GDP per capita, can lose everything with a natural disaster, as has happened, both in the Caribbean and in the Pacific, very frequently. So one cannot look only at the statistical dimension of GDP, it is important to look at vulnerability. And that is why this indicator I referred to, of multidimensional vulnerability, is so important, because it will allow whoever is in a development agency, in a donor country, whoever is in a development bank, whoever is in an investment bank, when they have to take financing decisions for countries, not to look only at GDP per capita, but to look also at the vulnerability of those countries. So the theme of international solidarity is crucial. And I sincerely believe that this summit managed to achieve historic levels of convergence with the SIDS agenda. Now it is necessary to move to action. And the United Nations agencies, such as UNOPS and the other agencies, obviously, have to be available for partnerships on the ground, to contribute to the delivery of projects, namely of infrastructure.

Ulisses Correia e Silva, in the intervention he made at the Summit, argued that the SIDS have to escape the trap of GDP per capita. Do you agree with that idea? Is GDP per capita really a trap?

I do not know whether it is a trap. It has been a metric that has not been sufficiently robust to deal with the small states under strain. So, in essence, we have metrics that, obviously, have to correspond to reality, and GDP per capita, which will have to continue to be used for many decisions, cannot be the only metric. That is why this multidimensional vulnerability indicator is a good contribution.

One last question. In the current political scenario at international level, with the emergence of extremist parties and governments and therefore less interested in international cooperation, is it possible to deliver this SIDS agenda?

In an increasingly interdependent world, we all gain from an increase in solidarity with the most vulnerable. The solution to the great global problems lies in more multilateralism and more cooperation and not in closure or intolerance.

Text originally published in the print edition of Expresso das Ilhas no. 1175 of 5 June 2024.

4G Passage of National Budget Draws Criticism -CENTAL Not Happy but Applauds Eligibility for MCC Compact
MONROVIA – One of Liberia’s outstanding civil society organizations, the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL, has criticized what it calls the “hasty passage” of Liberia’s national budget for 2025 fiscal period by the Legislature, stating it violates critical Liberian laws and best practices.
In its seasons message to the Liberian public, CENTAL noted that over the last two months, the House of Representatives has been embroiled with leadership struggle, which has significantly hamstrung the conduct of legislative activities, including the timely submission of the fiscal year 2025 National Budget by the President of the Republic of Liberia, through the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning.
The organization said besides the upheaval that has marred the Legislature, specifically the House of Representatives in the past couple of months, “we have seen nothing else from the people’s representatives, but a clamor for power and control over the country’s resources as well as claims and counterclaims of corruption.”
“During this period, perhaps worse than before, the lawmakers’ personal interests have superseded public interest,” CENTAL says, calling that in the midst of it all, on November 18, 2024, President Joseph N. Boakai submitted a draft 2025 national budget in the tone of US$851 million to the Chief Clerk of the House of Representatives.
Describing the submission as unprecedented, the organization stressed the review and discussion on the draft 2025 national budget and its passage happened in the period of ten days, and the worse of all that deliberations on the national budget were not presided over by the constitutionally-elected and sitting Speaker of the House of Representatives, but by a faction of Representatives with no authority to do so.
Assuming that the said faction acted with lawful authority, the group said, anyone can clearly see the lack of scrutiny as the budget was passed with lightning speed, with seemingly no objections to proposals from the Executive.
“It is our opinion, that only an illegitimate faction of the House seeking favors and recognition from the Executive would proceed in such a manner that admits of no oversight,” CENTAL also contends, further recalling that initial deliberations into the budget began on Monday, December 9, 2024, three weeks after it was submitted.
Said CENTAL in a release issued yesterday, noted that the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA), Liberia Maritime Authority (LMA), National Port Authority (NPA), and the Liberia Telecommunications Authority (LTA) were invited for discussions on the revenue component, and that about five days after, on Friday, December 13, 2024, the revenue component of the budget debate was exhausted, according to a dispatch from the Press Bureau of the House of Representatives.
Meanwhile, On Friday, December 20, 2024, about five working days after, the expenditure component of the budget was also declared exhausted and the budget, in the tone of US$880,662,000 was declared passed, CENTAL observed, adding: “On the same day, the Liberian Senate unanimously approved the budget, concurring with the House of Representatives’ earlier endorsement.”
The civil society organizations says it is deeply troubled by several missteps associated with the 2025 national budget submission and review process, which undermine its transparency and credibility and may have further implications for allocations to critical sectors, institutions and programs.
Notably, the group said, the executive branch submitted the draft national budget to the Legislature on November 18, 2024, something it says violates section 17.1 of the amended 2019 public financial management act, which requires submission of the draft budget no later than two months before the start of the fiscal year, January 1, 2025 in this instant case.
“In short, the submission process did not meet the two-month timeline provided for by the public financial management law of Liberia, thus allowing little time for review, deliberations, and passage/approval by the Legislature,” CENTAL charged. “Additionally, the 2025 National Budget did not undergo the required review and scrutiny, thus undermining its credibility and compliance with acceptable best practices and standards.”
The organization indicated that the Legislature begun public hearings on the draft budget on December 9, 2024 and approved it on December 20, 2024 means it did not thoroughly review and discuss the instrument, which contrasts with the Public Financial Management Laws that requires at least two months of intense review and discussions around the budget, whereby spending entities appear to present their plans and priorities as well as make convincing cases for increased funding.
“Besides, there is no publicly available information that the legislature thoroughly reviewed performance reports of the various spending entities, before approving their allocations in the current budget,” the accountability and transparency czar said, adding that a major check and balance, transparency and accountability gap, which undermine the oversight function of the legislature and leaves the use of public resources to the whims and caprices of public officials.
CENTAL use the statement to call on the Legislature to lead by example, as the direct representatives of the people, to set example of the adherence to the rule of law, including through respect for laid down procedures on deliberating on bills or removal of a sitting Speaker.
According to the organization, there can be no short-cut about rule of law and adherence to budgetary process, for all the mishaps could surely haunt the country in the not-too-distant future.
CENTAL emphasized that the actions of a certain group of lawmakers to assume the authority to pass the budget is a dangerous precedent as, going forward, any group of 38 lawmakers can gather together to make laws outside of established channels in so far as they have the backing of the Executive.
“We, therefore, call on President Joseph N. Boakai to distance himself from this illegal act by refusing to recognize same as a product of proper legislative enactment,” the group said. “We believe that this would not only allay concerns that the Presidency has been actively involved in undermining the sitting Speaker, but that it would also serve to safeguard the integrity of our budget process.”
On MCC Compact
Meanwhile CENTAL has welcomed Liberia’s eligibility for MCC Grant, saying it is a boast to the image of the country.
During its quarterly meeting on December 18, the Board of Directors of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) announced Liberia’s eligibility and selection for a new Compact, following the end of the previous compact in 2021.
Accordingly, Liberia was selected in recognition of the progress the country has made to strengthen its performance on the MCC scorecard and the country’s commitment to pursuing critical economic and democratic governance reforms.
CENTAL says it applauds the Liberian government for achieving this milestone, which presents the country with an opportunity to leverage resources to fund infrastructure and other critical sectors that will spur inclusive and sustainable economic growth and development, if properly and inclusively managed.
“We thank the US Government, through MCC, for this initiative and partnership and call for timely information sharing as well as meaningful civil society and citizens’ participation at all levels of Liberia’s Compact development, implementation, and monitoring processes,” the said civil society organization.
“We urge that successes, challenges, and lessons learned from the country’s past Compact inform decision-making around the new partnership, to ensure greater transparency, accountability, and inclusion of citizens and CSOs’ voices.”

a7071.t:
The Minister of Finance, Dr. Mwigulu Nchemba, has presented the budget framework and expenditure ceiling for the 2025/26 financial year to the Parliamentary Budget Committee in Dodoma.
The government plans to collect and spend TZS 57.04 trillion, marking a 13.4% increase from the 2024/25 budget, which stood at TZS 50.29 trillion.
The upcoming budget is the final one under the Tanzania Development Vision 2025. The government aims to generate 69.7% of its revenue from domestic sources to reduce reliance on unpredictable and high-cost conditional funding.
“The 2025/26 budget will be financed by TZS 40.97 trillion in revenue and TZS 16.07 trillion from domestic and foreign loans,” said Dr. Nchemba. “This includes TZS 31.83 trillion from tax revenue, TZS 6.23 trillion from non-tax revenue, TZS 1.68 trillion from local government revenues, and TZS 1.22 trillion from grants.”
He emphasized that the budget will support the final phase of the 2025 Development Vision and the 2025/26 Development Plan. Key spending priorities include debt servicing, the government wage bill, the general elections, strengthening democracy, maintaining peace and security, and preparations for the AFCON 2027 tournament.
Meanwhile, the Minister of State in the President’s Office for Planning and Investment, Prof. Kitila Mkumbo, addressed concerns about declining aid from developed nations. He reassured the parliamentary committee comprising all Members of Parliament that the government is prepared to mitigate the impact of reduced foreign aid.
“We are strengthening alternative financing mechanisms, such as public-private partnerships, to increase private sector participation in the economy,” said Prof. Mkumbo. “Honorable Members of Parliament need not worry. The government is fully committed to ensuring that reduced foreign aid strengthens our self-reliance and efficiency.”
The Parliament of the United Republic of Tanzania is expected to convene in the coming weeks to discuss and approve the budget and fiscal plans for 2025/26.

En signe de solidarité envers les victimes des récentes inondations qui ont frappé Gatumba,CRDB Bank Burundi, accompagné de plusieurs partenaires,a effectué une donation significative le samedi 24 mai 2025, pour soutenir plus de 1000 familles déplacées, actuellement relogées sur le site de Gateri de la commune Buganda en province de Cibitoke.
«Nous sommes venus auprès des habitants de Gatumba touchés par les inondations pour leur montrer qu’ils ne sont pas seuls», a déclaré Arnaud Rugema, représentant de CRDB Bank Burundi.Il a ensuite précisé que l’aide, constituée de 3 tonnes de riz, 3tonnes de haricots, de sorgho, de cahiers pour 480 élèves et de 500 kits d’ustensiles de cuisine, ainsi que d’une assistance financière, est le fruit de la collecte de fonds réalisée lors de la CRDB Marathon 2024,qui a permis de rassembler plus de 100 millions de francs burundais.« Cette initiative, a-t-il ajouté, aura lieu chaque année et CRDB Bank Burundi est prête à accompagner toute personne qui souhaitera développer des projets d’Autonomisation sur le site de Gateri.»
Pamphile Hakizimana, administrateur de la commune de Buganda, a exprimé sa profonde gratitude envers CRDB Bank Burundi et ses partenaires pour leur action en faveur des sinistrés. «Ces familles vivent grâce à l’aide humanitaire car elles n’ont plus de terres pour cultiver», a-t-il souligné. Il a ensuite encouragé vivement les bénéficiaires à utiliser cette assistance pour initier des petites activités génératrices de revenus, tell le commerce, afin de commencer leur reconstruction progressive.
Prenant la parole au nom des familles relogées à Gateri, Raphaël Nijimbere a également remercié chaleureusement les donateurs pour leur générosité et les autorités communales pour leur soutien dans leur réinstallation. «Nous vous sommes reconnaissants pour ce que vous nous avez apporté, ainsi qu’aux autorités de la commune Buganda qui nous ont montré comment nous installer. Nous sollicitons votre soutien continu pour que vous plaidiez notre cause afin que nous puissions bénéficier de formations professionnelles, apprendre les techniques agricoles, et que le gouvernement nous aide à obtenir des terres cultivables pour assurer notre subsistance», a-t-il plaidé.
Il a conclu en demandant l’assistance d’experts en construction pour bâtir des habitations durables, compte tenu de la nature rocailleuse du site qui rend le creusage difficile sans équipement approprié.
Cette action conjointe de CRDB Bank Burundi et de ses partenaires témoigne d’une solidarité essentielle envers la population vulnérable et offre une lueur d’espoir pour un avenir meilleur aux familles affectées par les inondations de Gatumba.
Jean Marie Ndayisenga (stagiaire)
a7143.en:
As a sign of solidarity with the victims of the recent floods that struck Gatumba, CRDB Bank Burundi, accompanied by several partners, made a significant donation on Saturday 24 May 2025 to support more than 1,000 displaced families, currently rehoused at the Gateri site in Buganda commune, Cibitoke province.

"We have come to the residents of Gatumba affected by the floods to show them that they are not alone," said Arnaud Rugema, representative of CRDB Bank Burundi. He then specified that the aid, consisting of 3 tonnes of rice, 3 tonnes of beans, sorghum, exercise books for 480 pupils and 500 kitchen utensil kits, as well as financial assistance, is the fruit of the fundraising carried out during the CRDB Marathon 2024, which made it possible to raise more than 100 million Burundian francs. "This initiative," he added, "will take place every year and CRDB Bank Burundi is ready to support anyone who wishes to develop empowerment projects at the Gateri site."

Pamphile Hakizimana, administrator of Buganda commune, expressed his deep gratitude to CRDB Bank Burundi and its partners for their action on behalf of the disaster victims. "These families live thanks to humanitarian aid because they no longer have land to cultivate," he stressed. He then strongly encouraged the beneficiaries to use this assistance to start small income-generating activities, such as trade, in order to begin their gradual reconstruction.

Speaking on behalf of the families rehoused at Gateri, Raphaël Nijimbere also warmly thanked the donors for their generosity and the communal authorities for their support in their resettlement. "We are grateful to you for what you have brought us, as well as to the authorities of Buganda commune who showed us how to settle in. We request your continued support so that you plead our cause so that we may benefit from vocational training, learn agricultural techniques, and so that the government helps us obtain arable land to ensure our subsistence," he pleaded.

He concluded by asking for the assistance of construction experts to build durable housing, given the rocky nature of the site, which makes digging difficult without appropriate equipment.

This joint action by CRDB Bank Burundi and its partners testifies to an essential solidarity towards the vulnerable population and offers a glimmer of hope for a better future for the families affected by the Gatumba floods.

Jean Marie Ndayisenga (intern)

a7241.t:
Centenas de trabalhadores de várias agências das Nações Unidas manifestaram-se em frente à sede europeia da ONU para protestar contra os cortes de pessoal que muitas das organizações internacionais estão a sofrer.
Sob o lema “O pessoal da ONU não é mercadoria” e “Defendemos a humanidade”, a manifestação contou com a participação da Public Services International (PSI), da Federação das Associações Internacionais de Funcionários Públicos (Ficsa) e do Comité Coordenador dos Sindicatos e Associações da ONU (Ccisua).
“Estamos numa situação muito difícil e infeliz, em que não são apenas os governos do mundo que estão a ser atacados, mas também a ONU e as suas agências”, afirmou o secretário-geral da PSI, Daniel Bertossa, na manifestação de protesto.
Segundo a agência EFE, a situação está a ser agravada pela retirada de grande parte da ajuda do seu principal contribuinte, o governo dos Estados Unidos.
“Não somos uma mercadoria, mas seres humanos que têm direito a boas condições de trabalho e ao respeito pela nossa dignidade”, acrescentou a presidente do sindicato dos trabalhadores da Organização Internacional do Trabalho (OIT), Severine Deboos.
Muitas das agências da ONU já estavam a sofrer crises orçamentais antes da chegada de Donald Trump, mas o regresso à Casa Branca do Presidente dos Estados Unidos, com uma atitude hostil ao multilateralismo, exacerbou os problemas e causou graves cortes no pessoal.
Na sequência do corte drástico na ajuda dos EUA, a Agência da ONU para os Refugiados (ACNUR) e o Programa Alimentar Mundial (PAM) reduziram o pessoal em todo o mundo em cerca de 30%, enquanto a OIT cortou 10% dos seus postos de trabalho, de acordo com os organizadores da manifestação.
Outras agências, como a Organização Mundial de Saúde (OMS), a Organização Internacional para as Migrações (OIM), a ONUSIDA e o Gabinete de Coordenação dos Assuntos Humanitários (OCHA) também foram obrigados a reduzir milhares de postos de trabalho, enquanto o Fundo das Nações Unidas para a Infância (UNICEF) viu o seu orçamento diminuir em 20%.
“Não são apenas estatísticas, por detrás delas estão milhares de pessoas que levam ajuda humanitária, asseguram o acesso à água potável, alimentos e cuidados de saúde, protegem os refugiados e as pessoas deslocadas, mantêm as crianças na escola, previnem o trabalho forçado e defendem os direitos humanos”, afirmaram as dirigentes da Ccisua e da Ficsa, Nathalie Meynet e Cristina Pierini.
a7241.en:
Hundreds of workers from various United Nations agencies demonstrated in front of the UN's European headquarters to protest against the staff cuts that many of the international organisations are undergoing.

Under the slogans "UN staff are not a commodity" and "We defend humanity", the demonstration was attended by Public Services International (PSI), the Federation of International Civil Servants' Associations (FICSA) and the Coordinating Committee of Unions and Associations of the UN System (CCISUA).

"We are in a very difficult and unfortunate situation, in which it is not only the world's governments that are being attacked, but also the UN and its agencies," said the General Secretary of PSI, Daniel Bertossa, at the protest demonstration.

According to the EFE news agency, the situation is being aggravated by the withdrawal of a large part of the aid from its main contributor, the government of the United States.

"We are not a commodity, but human beings who have a right to good working conditions and to respect for our dignity," added the president of the staff union of the International Labour Organization (ILO), Severine Deboos.

Many of the UN agencies were already suffering budget crises before the arrival of Donald Trump, but the return to the White House of the President of the United States, with an attitude hostile to multilateralism, exacerbated the problems and caused severe staff cuts.

Following the drastic cut in US aid, the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the World Food Programme (WFP) have reduced staff worldwide by around 30%, while the ILO cut 10% of its jobs, according to the organisers of the demonstration.

Other agencies, such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the International Organization for Migration (IOM), UNAIDS and the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) have also been forced to cut thousands of jobs, while the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) saw its budget shrink by 20%.

"These are not just statistics; behind them are thousands of people who deliver humanitarian aid, ensure access to drinking water, food and health care, protect refugees and displaced people, keep children in school, prevent forced labour and defend human rights," said the leaders of CCISUA and FICSA, Nathalie Meynet and Cristina Pierini.
